questions.answer_text: The "basic structure" doctrine was brought into existence by the Supreme Court to protect the fundamental features of the Constitution.
questions.explanation: The Basic Structure Doctrine is a judicial principle evolved in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). The Supreme Court held that while Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368, it cannot alter or destroy its “basic structure”. This doctrine safeguards the core identity and fundamental features of the Constitution from being undermined by a temporary majority in Parliament.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: According to Section 21 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which of the following statements is correct regarding the trial of offences under Sections 64 to 71 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

options.a: The trial must be conducted by any police officer of the rank of DSP and above.
options.b: These offences must be tried only in a High Court under a male judge.
options.c: Such offences are exclusively triable by Executive Magistrates.
options.d: These offences shall, as far as practicable, be tried by a court presided over by a woman.

questions.answer_text: These offences shall, as far as practicable, be tried by a court presided over by a woman.
questions.explanation: According to Section 21 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, offences covered under Sections 64 to 71 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023—which relate to crimes against women such as sexual offences—are to be handled with sensitivity and care. The law states that such offences shall, as far as practicable, be tried by a court presided over by a woman. This provision aims to ensure a more empathetic and comfortable environment for victims during the trial process, promoting gender sensitivity and improving the judicial experience for women seeking justice.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following High Courts has jurisdiction over more than one state?
questions.explanation: Guwahati High Court. The Guwahati High Court (established in 1948) originally had jurisdiction over the entire Northeast region. At present, it has jurisdiction over Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh. Other Northeastern states such as Manipur, Meghalaya, and Tripura now have their own separate High Courts (established in 2013). Kerala High Court – Has jurisdiction only over Kerala and the Union Territory of Lakshadweep. Delhi High Court – Jurisdiction is limited to the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi. Patna High Court – Jurisdiction is only over the state of Bihar.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India?

options.a: Article 30 of the Constitution of India gives the Supreme Court wide original jurisdiction.
options.b: Original jurisdiction extends to any dispute between the Government of India and one or more states.
options.c: The Supreme Court has very wide advisory jurisdiction over all courts and tribunals in India.
options.d: The original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court can be exercised by a certificate granted by the High Court.

questions.answer_text: Original jurisdiction extends to any dispute between the Government of India and one or more states.
questions.explanation: According to Article 131 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court has original jurisdiction over any dispute arising between the Government of India and one or more States.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the first-ever motion to remove a Supreme Court Justice in India: A. The first motion to remove a Supreme Court Judge was signed in 1991 by 108 Members of Parliament. B. It was filed against Justice V. Ramaswami for alleged misconduct during his tenure as Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court. Which one of the above statements is correct?
questions.explanation: Only A. The first motion to remove a Supreme Court Justice was signed in 1991 by 108 MPs against Justice V. Ramaswami. He was accused of financial and administrative misconduct during his tenure as Chief Justice of the Punjab and Haryana High Court (1987–1989), not the Allahabad High Court.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India grants power to the President to appoint Judges of the Supreme Court?
questions.explanation: Article 124(2). It states that every Supreme Court judge is appointed by the President through a warrant, after consulting judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as deemed necessary. Judges hold office until the age of sixty-five. Additionally, the Chief Justice of India must always be consulted for the appointment of judges other than the Chief Justice.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Supreme Court of India comprises the Chief Justice and not more than ______ other Judges appointed by the President of India.
questions.explanation: 33. The judges of supreme court are appointed by the president under the Article 124 (2) of the Indian Constitution. Supreme Court Judges retire at the age of 65. As per Article 124 (3) - In order to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court, a person must be a citizen of India and must have been, for at least five years, a Judge of a High Court or an Advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years or he must be, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Constitution: A. Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI deal with the High Courts in the states. B. These Articles provide for the organization, independence, jurisdiction, powers, and procedures of the High Courts. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI of the Indian Constitution deal with the High Courts in the states, covering their establishment, powers, jurisdiction, independence, and functioning.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which writ is issued by a high court or supreme court when a lower court has considered a case going beyond its jurisdiction?
questions.explanation: Prohibition. Writs are issued by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by the High Court under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution. The five types of writs in India are: Habeas Corpus: Ensures that a detained person is brought before the court. Mandamus: Directs a public official to perform a duty. Certiorari: Transfers a case for review by a higher court. Prohibition: Prevents a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction. Quo-Warranto: Questions the legal authority of someone holding a public office.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which judgement did the Supreme Court extend the scope of Article 21 and observed that ‘the Right to education flows directly from the ‘Right to life’ ?

options.a: Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka
options.b: Neerja Choudhari v State of M. P.
options.c: Kharak Singh v State of UP
options.d: Malak Singh v State of Punjab

questions.answer_text: Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka
questions.explanation: Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka. The Supreme Court declared that it was impermissible for any educational institution to charge capitation fees as a consideration for admission. Neeraja Chaudhary vs. State of Madhya Pradesh - addressed the issue of bonded labor. Kharak Singh v State of UP - focused on the constitutional review of Uttar Pradesh Police Regulations.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution mentions that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all the courts within the territory of India?
questions.explanation: Article 141. Other Articles: Article 137 - Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court. Article 147 - Any substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution shall be construed as including references to any substantial question of law as to the interpretation. Article 151 - Audit reports.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India? A. Original jurisdiction extends to any dispute between the Government of India and one or more States or between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more States on the other or between two or more States. B. Appellate Jurisdiction extends when the Union plus some States are one side and some other States on the other side of the dispute. C. Under Articles 129 and 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has been vested with the power to punish for contempt of court. D. As of now, the International Commercial Arbitration cannot be initiated in the Supreme Court.
questions.explanation: A and C only. Advisory Jurisdiction (Article 143) - The President to seek the opinion of the Supreme Court. The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court can be invoked by a certificate granted by the High Court concerned under Article 132(1), 133(1) or 134 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court (Article 124) of India is the apex judicial body under the Constitution of India. Inaugurated - On January, 28, 1950.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The advisory board under provisions of Article 22 of the Constitution is to consist of persons who are, or have been or are qualified to be appointed as __________.
questions.explanation: Judges of High court. Related Articles : Article 214 - High Courts for States. Article 215 - High Courts to be courts of record. Article 216 - Constitution of High Courts. Article 217 - Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court. Article 218 - Application of certain provisions relating to the Supreme Court to High Courts. Article 219 - Oath or affirmation by Judges of High Courts. Article 220 - Restriction on practice after being a permanent Judge.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Federal Court of India: A. The Federal Court of India was established in Delhi under the Government of India Act, 1935, and started functioning from 1937. B. It served as the highest judicial body in India until it was replaced by the Supreme Court of India in 1950. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. The Federal Court of India was set up under the Government of India Act, 1935, and began functioning in 1937. It was created to resolve disputes between provinces and federal states and remained active until 1950, when the Supreme Court of India replaced it. Calcutta High Court (1862) is the oldest High Court in India, and Justice Harilal Jekisundas Kania was the first Chief Justice of independent India.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Supreme Court of India: A. Article 124 of the Indian Constitution provides that there shall be a Supreme Court of India. B. Article 121 deals with restrictions on discussion in Parliament regarding the conduct of judges of the Supreme Court or a High Court. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court of India, laying down its structure and provisions for appointment of judges. Article 121 restricts Parliament from discussing the conduct of Supreme Court or High Court judges except during impeachment proceedings. Article 122 states that courts cannot inquire into parliamentary proceedings.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Disputes between two or more states come under the _______ of the Supreme Court.
questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction - The power to hear and determine a dispute in the first instance. It is provided under Article 131 of the Indian Constitution. Article 143 of the Indian Constitution confers upon the Supreme Court advisory jurisdiction. Article 133 - Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in regard to civil matters.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which of the following cases the Supreme Court, while laying out the 'basic structure' of the Constitution held that the democratic character of the polity was an essential component of the 'basic structure" ?

options.a: Romesh Thappar vs State of Madras
options.b: AK Gopalan vs State of Madras
options.c: Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala
options.d: Sajjan Singh vs State of Rajasthan

questions.answer_text: Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala
questions.explanation: This judgement was delivered on 24 April 1973. The case was filed by Sri Kesavananda Bharati (head of a Hindu religious mutt in Kerala), challenging the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments to the Indian Constitution. Romesh Thappar vs State of Madras: Freedom of speech and expression includes Freedom of press. AK Gopalan vs State of Madras - Deals with the constitutionality of preventive detention. Sajjan Singh vs State of Rajasthan - Involved a challenge to the validity of the Constitution (26th Amendment) Act.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding important Supreme Court judgments: A. In the State of Kerala vs Leesamma Joseph case, the Supreme Court held that persons with disabilities are entitled to reservation in promotions under Article 16. B. In the Shayara Bano vs Union of India case, the Supreme Court struck down the practice of triple talaq as unconstitutional. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. The Leesamma Joseph case recognized reservation in promotions for persons with disabilities under Article 16, ensuring equal opportunity in employment. The Shayara Bano case (2017) declared instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) unconstitutional, reinforcing gender justice and equality. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) laid down the Basic Structure Doctrine of the Constitution.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Supreme Court of India came into existence on ___________ .
questions.explanation: 26 January 1950. The Supreme Court was inaugurated in the Chamber of Princes in the Parliament House on January 28, 1950. The foundation stone of the Supreme Court building was laid by the first President of India, Rajendra Prasad, on October 29, 1954. The 50th Chief Justice of India is Dhananjaya Y. Chandrachud.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Till which year did the High Court of Delhi continue to exercise jurisdiction over Himachal Pradesh?
questions.explanation: 1971. The Indian High Courts Act (1861) established High Courts of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay. The first high court of India was established in Kolkata and formally it was called the High Court of Judicature at Fort William. India has 25 High Courts (now). Article 214 - High Court for each State. Article 226 - Power of high court to issue certain writs. Article 216 - Constitution of High Court.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following statements are true regarding the Family Courts (Amendment) Bill, 2022? 1. The Family Courts (Amendment) Bill was introduced in Lok Sabha on 18 July 2022. 2. The Bill amends the Family Courts Act, 1984. 3. The Act allows state governments to establish Family Courts. 4. The Act is not applicable in Punjab and Tamil Nadu.
questions.explanation: 1, 2 and 3. Family Courts (Amendment) Bill 2022 seeks to amend the Family Courts Act, 1984 to establish family courts in Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland. Family Court Act, 1984 - Enacted for the establishment of Family Courts with a view to promote conciliation, and secure speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage and family affairs and for related matters.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The High court of Delhi was established in _______.
questions.explanation: 1966. The High Court of Delhi was established with four Judges. They were Chief Justice K.S.Hegde, Justice I.D. Dua, Justice H.R.Khanna and Justice S.K.Kapur. Before 1966 under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 Delhi was under the jurisdiction of the Punjab High Court.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The first High Court in India was established in ______________ .
questions.explanation: 1862. Calcutta High Court: It was brought into existence under the High Court's Act (1861). Location - Esplanade Row West (Kolkata). Jurisdiction - West Bengal and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Bombay High Court {(14 August 1862) (Indian High Courts Act 1861)}, Madras High Court {(15 August 1862, Indian High Courts Act 1861}.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court of India pronounce the theory of the ‘Basic Structure’ of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Kesavananda Bharati Case, 1973 - Parliament can not amend or alter the ‘Basic Structure’ of the constitution. Golaknath Case, 1967 - Parliament cannot take away or abridge any of the Fundamental Rights. Minerva Mills Case, 1980 - Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but it cannot change the “Basic Structure” of the Constitution. Swarn Singh Case, 1998 - In this case, the SC held the UP Governor's pardon of a convict unconstitutional.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the structure of the Indian judiciary: A. The Supreme Court is at the top, High Courts are in the middle, and subordinate courts are at the bottom. B. The Indian judiciary follows a three-tier unified system. Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. The judiciary in India has a three-tier structure: the Supreme Court (Article 124) at the top, High Courts (Article 214) at the state level, and subordinate courts (district and sessions courts) at the bottom, making it a unified system.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed only on the grounds of ______.
questions.explanation: Proven misbehaviour or incapacity. Article 124 - There shall be a Supreme Court of India. Article 143 - Power of the President to consult the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India: A. The Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Article 131) allows it to settle disputes between the Centre and States, and among States. B. The Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Article 143) deals with disputes between the Union and the States. Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation: A only. The Original Jurisdiction (Article 131) empowers the Supreme Court to adjudicate disputes between the Centre and States or among States. The Advisory Jurisdiction (Article 143) only enables the President to seek the Court’s opinion, not to decide such disputes.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: A Supreme Court or High Court judge can be removed by the Parliament by:

options.b: both simple and two third majority

questions.explanation: Special majority. Special majority as per Article 249 requires a majority of 2/3rd members present and voting. For example, if out of the 245 members in Rajya Sabha, only 150 are present and voting, then the special majority required as per Article 249 would be 101. Simple majority refers to a majority of more than 50% of the members present and voting in the House. Majorities in the Constitution can be categorised into four Types : Absolute, Effective, Simple and Special.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which is NOT correct about the independence of the judiciary in our country?

options.a: The judiciary has the power to penalise those who are found guilty of contempt of court.
options.b: The judges are financially dependent on both the executive and legislature for their salaries and allowances.
options.c: The Constitution prescribes a very difficult procedure for removal of judges.
options.d: The legislature is not involved in the process of appointment of judges.

questions.answer_text: The judges are financially dependent on both the executive and legislature for their salaries and allowances.
questions.explanation: Judges salaries and allowances are fixed and not subject to legislative approval. Supreme Court Judges {The Salaries, Pension and Allowances are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266 (1)}, High Court Judges {Salaries and Allowances are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of the States and the Pension is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India} .

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Indian judicial system is based on:
questions.explanation: single integrated system. The judiciary is the watchdog of democracy, and also the guardian of the Constitution. Structure of Indian Judiciary {Supreme Court at the top, High Courts are below the SC, and below them are the district and subordinate courts}.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following commissions is NOT a statutory body in India ?
questions.explanation: National Commission for Farmers. A statutory body is one created by a law (Act of Parliament/State Legislature). National Commission for Farmers (NCF) – set up in 2004 as an advisory body/committee under M.S. Swaminathan (not statutory, only an expert commission). National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) – statutory body under Article 338A, established through the 89th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) – Statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. National Commission for Women (NCW) – statutory body under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)? 1. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita introduces community service as a punishment for minor offences. 2. The scope of summary trials has been limited to only serious offences under the new law. 3. The reformative approach aims to ensure societal reintegration of offenders.
questions.explanation: 1 and 3 only. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 is India's new criminal code, enacted to replace the colonial-era Indian Penal Code (IPC) of 1860, with provisions coming into effect from July 1, 2024. It introduces community service as punishment for minor offences (Statement 1) and adopts a reformative approach to help offenders reintegrate into society (Statement 3). However, the scope of summary trials has been expanded to more petty offences, not limited to serious ones.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Given below are two statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). questions.subject: Polity

questions.answer_text: To verify citizenship claims of individuals excluded from the NRC
questions.explanation: Foreigners' Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies, established under the Foreigners' Act of 1946 and Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964, to determine if a person suspected of being a foreigner is, in fact, one.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: What is the role of the finance minister under the FRBM Act?

options.d: To present fiscal policy statements to Parliament

questions.answer_text: To present fiscal policy statements to Parliament
questions.explanation: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, was enacted to ensure fiscal discipline, transparency, and accountability in the government's financial operations. A key requirement under this Act is that the Union Finance Minister must, along with the annual Union Budget, present the following three statements before both Houses of Parliament: The Macro-Economic Framework Statement; The Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement; and The Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement. These documents provide a transparent overview of the government's fiscal position and its roadmap for achieving targets related to fiscal deficit, revenue deficit, and public debt.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes the statutory responsibilities of the Lokpal under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013?

options.a: The Lokpal is mandated to provide the President with an annual report, which will be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
options.b: The Lokpal operates under the direct administrative control of the Prime Minister's Office.
options.c: The Lokpal must submit regular reports to the Election Commission for public disclosure.
options.d: The Lokpal is a constitutional body tasked with making final judgments in corruption cases.

questions.answer_text: The Lokpal is mandated to provide the President with an annual report, which will be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
questions.explanation: Under Section 48 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Lokpal is mandated to submit an annual performance report to the President of India, who must then place it before both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha for parliamentary scrutiny and transparency. The Lokpal, established as an independent statutory body under Section 3 of the Act, serves as a dedicated anti-corruption authority, functioning free from executive influence.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Statutory grants to states by the Union government, under Article 275 of the Constitution, are primarily recommended by which body?

These grants are given to help states meet the costs of schemes for welfare of Scheduled Tribes, administration of Scheduled Areas, and other special needs. The Finance Commission (constituted every 5 years under Article 280) recommends: Distribution of net tax proceeds between Centre and States. Grants-in-aid of revenues of the states under Article 275. Measures to improve fiscal stability.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Election Commission of India founded?

questions.question: UPSC is a Constitutional Body to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Union and the services of the State, respectively, under Article ________

Article 328 grants state legislatures the authority to create provisions for elections to their respective legislatures, including the preparation of electoral rolls, delimitation of constituencies, and other arrangements for the constitution of the legislature. Article 332 reserves seats in state legislative assemblies for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding Public Service Commissions in India: A. The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) functions as the central recruitment agency, while each State has its own Public Service Commission. B. The establishment of Union, State, and Joint Public Service Commissions reflects the federal character of the Indian Constitution. Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. UPSC, SPSC, and Joint PSC are constitutional bodies, and their existence represents the federal principle by dividing recruitment functions between the Union and the States.

questions.question: The Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India comes under the:

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Who among the following are eligible for free legal aid under the National Legal Services Authority? A. A member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe. B. options.a: A, B, C and D only
options.d: A, B, C, D and E

questions.answer_text: A, B, C and D only
questions.explanation: A, B, C and D only. According to the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), the following individuals are eligible for free legal aid: women and children, mentally ill or disabled persons, and victims of mass disasters, violence, floods, droughts, earthquakes, and industrial disasters. options.b: a Chairperson and three other members

options.a: The National Commission for Women Act, 1988
options.b: The National Commission for Women Act, 1990

questions.answer_text: The National Commission for Women Act, 1990
questions.explanation: The National Commission for Women is a statutory body set up in January 1992 under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990 to review the constitutional and legal safeguards for women; recommend remedial legislative measures; facilitate redressal of grievances and advise the Government on all policy matters affecting women. questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the State Election Commissioner (SEC) in India: A. The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor of the state. B. The SEC is responsible for conducting free, fair, and impartial elections to local bodies in the state. Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. The Governor appoints the State Election Commissioner (SEC) under Article 243K (for Panchayats) and Article 243ZA (for Municipalities). The SEC is responsible for conducting free, fair, and impartial elections to local bodies in the state. The SEC functions independently and cannot be removed from office except in the manner and on the grounds prescribed for a High Court judge, ensuring autonomy and fairness in the electoral process.

questions.explanation: Election Commission - established in 1950. Part XV Election Commission (324 - 329): Article 326 - Elections to the House of the People and to the Legislative Assemblies of States to be on the basis of adult suffrage.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In India, which Ministry issues the coins of all denominations ?
questions.explanation: Ministry of Finance. The Government of India has the sole right to mint coins. The responsibility for coinage vests with the Government of India in accordance with the Coinage Act, 1906 as amended from time to time. The designing and minting of coins in various denominations is also the responsibility of the Government of India. Coins are minted at the four Indian Government Mints at Mumbai, Alipore (Kolkata), Saifabad (Hyderabad), Cherlapally (Hyderabad) and Noida (UP). It is issued for circulation only through the Reserve Bank in terms of the RBI Act.

The ECI body administers elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, State Legislative Councils and the offices of the President and the Vice President of the country.

questions.explanation: 2015. Nepal's first democratic constitution came into effect on Sept 20, 2015. The constitution of Nepal is divided into 35 parts, 308 Articles, and 9 Schedules.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which principle of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 ensures that entities collecting personal data must obtain explicit consent from individuals ?
questions.explanation: Notice and Choice Framework. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDPA) is India’s landmark law on safeguarding personal data. The Notice and Choice Framework ensures that entities (called Data Fiduciaries) must provide individuals (Data Principals) with a clear notice of what data is being collected, why it is being collected, and how it will be used. It also requires obtaining explicit and informed consent from individuals before processing their personal data.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of these is not a feature of Indian federalism?
questions.explanation: Dual Citizenship. India provides single citizenship for all its citizens, unlike countries like the USA which follow dual citizenship under federalism. Other features of Indian federalism include a written constitution, independent judiciary, and clear division of powers.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: What is the punishment for abetment of an offense under the POCSO Act?

options.b: Half the punishment prescribed for the offense

questions.explanation: Same punishment as the offense. Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, abetment of an offense is treated with the same gravity as the actual commission of the offense. Section 16 of the Act defines abetment, and Section 17 prescribes that anyone who abets a POCSO offense shall be punished with the same punishment as is provided for the offense itself. This strict provision ensures that those who encourage, assist, or facilitate crimes against children are held equally accountable, thereby strengthening child protection.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: If "a soldier fires on a mob by the order of his superior officer, in conformity with the law". According to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, has he committed an offence?

options.a: Yes, because he could have disobeyed
options.c: No, because he followed public orders
options.d: No, because he believed in good faith that he was bound by law

questions.answer_text: No, because he believed in good faith that he was bound by law
questions.explanation: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (earlier IPC Section 76), an act done by a person who believes in good faith that they are bound by law is not an offence. A soldier acting under lawful orders of a superior, in conformity with the law, is protected from criminal liability.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements: Statement I: Land and agriculture fall under the State List. Statement II: Marriage laws and adoption fall under the Concurrent List. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

options.c: Both statements I and II are correct
options.d: Neither statement I nor II is correct

questions.answer_text: Both statements I and II are correct
questions.explanation: Both statements I and II are correct. Subjects like land, rights in land, land revenue, agriculture, agricultural education & research are placed in the State List under the 7th Schedule of the Indian Constitution. Matters like marriage, divorce, infants, minors, adoption, succession, transfer of property are in the Concurrent List. This allows both Parliament and State legislatures to make laws (e.g., Hindu Marriage Act, Special Marriage Act).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The new criminal laws aim to replace British-era laws with a focus on:
questions.explanation: New Criminal Laws (Effective from July 1, 2024): Replaced the British-era laws: Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860 → Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023. Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973 → Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023. Indian Evidence Act, 1872 → Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023. Main Focus: Justice delivery over punishment. Protection of citizen rights. Speedier trials, use of technology, stronger provisions against crimes like terrorism, mob lynching, crimes against women and children. Ending colonial legacy and making laws more citizen-centric.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Under Chapter V of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which of the following qualifies as primary evidence?

options.a: A counterpart document executed by one of the parties
options.b: A photocopy of the document signed by a clerk
options.d: A typed copy of the original document

questions.answer_text: A counterpart document executed by one of the parties
questions.explanation: Under Section 57 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, primary evidence is defined as the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court. Explanation 2 of this section clarifies that when a document is executed in counterpart, with each counterpart being signed by one or some of the parties, each counterpart is considered primary evidence against the party who executed it.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: What is the maximum time limit for completing the trial of a case under the POCSO Act?
questions.explanation: 1 year. Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, the law mandates that the trial for any offence under the Act should be completed within one year from the date the court takes cognizance of the case. This time-bound trial provision is aimed at delivering swift justice to child victims of sexual offences, minimizing their trauma and ensuring the justice system is sensitive to their needs. The Act recognizes the vulnerability of children and thus puts emphasis on a child-friendly, efficient, and expeditious legal process.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which discretionary power allows a Governor to reserve a bill passed by the state legislature for the consideration of the President?

options.a: To send a report to the President for the imposition of President's Rule.
options.b: To reserve a bill for the President's consideration.
options.c: To grant pardon in certain cases.
options.d: To summon, prorogue, and dissolve the state legislative assembly.

questions.answer_text: To reserve a bill for the President's consideration.
questions.explanation: To reserve a bill for the President's consideration. Under Article 200 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor has the discretionary power to reserve certain state bills for the consideration of the President. While most bills are assented to by the Governor, in specific cases (especially those that may conflict with central laws, affect national interest, or fall under the ambit of Article 31A, 31C, etc.), the Governor may choose to withhold assent and refer the bill to the President.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the implementation challenges of UCC is most accurate in the context of judicial interpretations and recent state-level developments?

options.a: UCC is enforceable only when ratified by all religious communities through a national referendum.
options.b: The Law Commission of India (2018) recommended UCC for all religions to ensure uniformity.
options.c: The Supreme Court has uniformly declared UCC as mandatory across states.
options.d: The UCC is already implemented in Goa and Uttarakhand through their respective legislative frameworks.

questions.answer_text: The UCC is already implemented in Goa and Uttarakhand through their respective legislative frameworks.
questions.explanation: The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) has been discussed in multiple Supreme Court judgments as a directive principle but has not been made mandatory across India. The 2018 Law Commission stated that a UCC was neither necessary nor desirable at that stage, instead suggesting reforms within personal laws. Goa already follows a Portuguese Civil Code, functioning as a form of UCC, and Uttarakhand passed its own UCC legislation in 2024, marking the first state to do so under Indian law.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: As per the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which of the following best defines "electronic communication"?

options.a: Any information transmitted using electronic devices like phones or computers
options.b: Only video calls conducted through secure government networks
options.d: Verbal messages sent through written documents only

questions.answer_text: Any information transmitted using electronic devices like phones or computers
questions.explanation: According to Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, "electronic communication" is broadly defined as the transmission of any written, verbal, pictorial information, or video content using electronic devices. This includes devices like telephones, mobile phones, computers, and any other electronic means specified by the government. The definition is comprehensive, covering various forms of digital information exchange.

questions.question: Which of the following best reflects the constitutional dilemma in implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in India, as discussed in debates surrounding Article 44 and Article 25?

options.a: UCC allows gender-based personal law systems to remain untouched under Article 14
options.b: UCC enforces cooperative federalism by giving states legislative powers on personal law
options.c: UCC operationalises the secular ethos by completely eliminating all religious laws
options.d: UCC aligns with Article 44 but may be seen to infringe upon religious freedom under Article 25

questions.answer_text: UCC aligns with Article 44 but may be seen to infringe upon religious freedom under Article 25
questions.explanation: Article 44 (Directive Principle): Directs the State to endeavor to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens, promoting unity and gender justice by replacing religion-based personal laws with a common set of rules. Article 25 (Fundamental Right): Guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion. The dilemma: Implementing UCC ensures equality (Article 14) and fulfills Article 44’s directive, but it may be perceived as restricting Article 25 if it overrides religious practices tied to personal laws (marriage, divorce, succession, etc.).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the below statements: 1. Governor is state's constitutional head. 2. He acts solely on Council's advice. Which of the above statements holds true regarding Governor's executive powers?
questions.explanation: Only 1. Statement 1 – Correct. The Governor is the constitutional head of the state (Article 153). Just as the President is the head of the Union, the Governor is the head of the State Executive. Statement 2 – Incorrect. The Governor is required to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister (Article 163). However, he does not act solely on their advice. In certain matters, he exercises discretionary powers (e.g., reserving bills for the President, recommending President’s Rule under Article 356, appointment of CM in a hung assembly, etc.).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Under Section 25(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, what may the Court do when a person is convicted in one trial for multiple offences?

options.a: Can impose only one punishment for all the offences, regardless of their nature
options.b: Must give the harshest punishment only and remit other punishments altogether
options.c: Shall suspend all sentences unless directed by a higher court in the same trial
options.d: May impose punishments to run either concurrently or consecutively as appropriate

questions.answer_text: May impose punishments to run either concurrently or consecutively as appropriate
questions.explanation: Section 25(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 deals with the sentencing in cases where a person is convicted of two or more offences in the same trial. It empowers the Court to: Award punishments for each offence separately. Direct that the punishments may run concurrently (at the same time) or consecutively (one after the other), depending on the facts of the case and judicial discretion. This provision is similar to Section 31(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of newly created States/Union Territories after the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Chhattisgarh - 2000. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 reorganized Indian states on linguistic basis. After that, several new states were created in later years through separate legislations: Chhattisgarh - Created on 1st November 2000, carved out of Madhya Pradesh. Jharkhand - Created on 15th November 2000, carved out of Bihar (not 2001). Uttarakhand - Created on 9th November 2000 as Uttaranchal (renamed Uttarakhand in 2007), not 1998. Telangana - Created on 2nd June 2014, carved out of Andhra Pradesh (not 2001).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which Indian state does S. Jaishankar represent in the Rajya Sabha?
questions.explanation: Gujarat. He was first elected to the Rajya Sabha in 2019 from Gujarat and re-elected in 2023 for his second term, again representing Gujarat. Gujarat elects 11 members to the Rajya Sabha (the upper house of India's Parliament), who are chosen indirectly by the state's Legislative Assembly members. Additionally, as part of overall Parliamentary representation, Gujarat holds 26 Lok Sabha seats (the lower house), making a total of 37 directly or indirectly elected MPs from the state.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: On which date did Punjab abolish the Legislative Council?
questions.explanation: 1 January 1970. The Punjab Legislative Council (Abolition) Act, 1969 abolished the Legislative Council of Punjab, leading to the cessation of its members' positions. It amended Article 168 of the Constitution, removing reference to Punjab, and made changes to the Representation of the People Act, 1950.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the ‘Rule of Law’ in the Indian Constitution: A. The ‘Rule of Law’ is a key feature of the Indian Constitution and is a doctrine ascribed to Albert Venn Dicey. B. Plato, Adam Smith, and Karl Marx are not associated with the doctrine of the Rule of Law. Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. The Rule of Law, a fundamental principle in the Indian Constitution, was popularized by Albert Venn Dicey, a British jurist. Plato, Adam Smith, and Karl Marx contributed to philosophy, economics, and political theory, but not specifically to the doctrine of the Rule of Law.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The National Population Register was created under the provisions of ___________ and ___________ . a. the Citizenship Act, 1965 b. the Citizenship Rules, 2004 c. the Citizenship Act, 1955 d. the Citizenship Rules, 2003
questions.explanation: c; d. The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides for the acquisition and loss of citizenship after the commencement of the Constitution. Originally, the Act 1955 also provided for Commonwealth Citizenship. But, this provision was repealed by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which party formed the government in Britain in the year 1945?
questions.explanation: Labour Party. In the 1945 general elections in Britain, the Labour Party, under the leadership of Clement Attlee, achieved a decisive victory, defeating Winston Churchill's Conservative Party. Democratic Party is one of the two major political parties, alongside the Republican Party, in the United States.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The concept of Public Interest Litigation originated in _______________.
questions.explanation: USA. Public Interest Litigation (PIL) means litigation filed in a court of law, for the protection of “Public Interest”, such as Pollution, Terrorism, Road safety, Constructional hazards etc. The concept of PIL was initially sown in India by Justice Krishna Iyer, in 1976 in Mumbai Kamagar Sabha vs. Abdul Thai.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described Directive Principles of State Policy as __________of the Indian constitution.

options.c: The most precious part of the constitution
options.d: a novel feature of the constitution

questions.answer_text: a novel feature of the constitution
questions.explanation: a novel feature of the Indian

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which of the following years was the Right of Persons with Disabilities Act passed?
questions.explanation: 2016. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act came into force from 19th April, 2017. It replaced the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995. Objective - To ensure that all persons with disabilities can lead their lives with dignity, without discrimination and with equal opportunities.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: When did a States Reorganisation Commission was set up, which recommended the creation of linguistic States on the basis of larger linguistic groups?
questions.explanation: December 1953. India faced demands to reorganise states based on regional languages after independence. In November 1956, India underwent division into 14 states and six union territories through the implementation of the State Reorganisation Act. The Andhra State held the distinction of being the first state of Independent India, and it was later transformed into Andhra Pradesh on the 1st of November 1956. The State Reorganisation Commission was chaired by Fazal Ali, and two other members, namely K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following states is one of those states that have no Panchayati Raj Institution at all?
questions.explanation: Nagaland. Panchayats (Part IX, Articles 243 to 243-O): It is the system of local self-government of villages in rural India. Rajasthan was the first state to implement Panchayati Raj in India (on October 2nd, 1959, in Nagaur district), followed by Andhra Pradesh later in 1959. 24th April - National Panchayati Raj Day. Currently, the Panchayati Raj system exists in all states except Nagaland, Meghalaya, and Mizoram, and in all Union Territories except Delhi.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Citizenship Act, 1955 does NOT deal with ____________.
questions.explanation: election. The Citizenship Act, 1955 deals with the acquisition, determination, and termination of Indian citizenship. Citizenship Acquisition: The Act provides for the acquisition of citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory. Citizenship Determination: The Act defines how to determine Indian citizenship. Citizenship Termination: The Act provides for the termination and deprivation of citizenship. Election Commission of India: PART XV (Article 324-329) of the Constitution.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which Section of the Representation of People’s Act (RPA), 1951 deprives the prisoners of their right to vote?
questions.explanation: Section 62 (5) : A person cannot vote in an election if they are in prison or in police custody. However, this rule does not apply to those in preventive detention. Even if someone cannot vote due to imprisonment, they still remain an elector if their name is on the electoral roll.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The proclamation of which Act by the King of England in 1773 paved the way for the establishment of the Supreme Court at Calcutta?
questions.explanation: Regulating Act. The Regulating Act of 1773 led to the establishment of the Supreme Court at Calcutta, which included a chief justice (Elijah Impey) and three other judges. An amendment in 1781 exempted the Governor-General, the Council, and government officials from its jurisdiction while performing their duties.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which directive principle has been implemented in establishing Handloom and Handicrafts Boards?

options.a: Participation of workers in management of Industries
options.b: Provision for just and humane condition of work
options.d: Promote cottage industries on cooperative basis

questions.answer_text: Promote cottage industries on cooperative basis
questions.explanation: The All India Handloom Board (AIHB) and the All India Handicrafts Board (AIHB) were two boards in India aimed to promote and develop cottage industries, such as handlooms and handicrafts, through cooperative efforts and support. The All India Handicrafts Board was set up in 1952 whereas the All India Handloom Board was established in 1992. However, the government decided to abolish the board in 2020 as part of its vision of "Minimum Government and Maximum Governance".

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which south-eastern Dravidian language has been approved by Odisha state to be included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India, on 10th July 2023 ?
questions.explanation: Kui. It is spoken by the Kandhas community. It is closely related to the Gondi and Kuvi languages. Some other languages included in the eighth schedule are: Sindhi was introduced in 1967. Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali in 1992. Santali, Dogri, Maithili, and Bodo in 2003.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following organisation’s initiative is ‘India Justice Report’?
questions.explanation: Tata Trusts. The India Justice Report (IJR) is an initiative by Tata Trusts, in collaboration with the Centre for Social Justice, Common Cause, and the Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative, among others. It was first published in 2019. Karnataka was the top-ranked state in the 2022 India Justice Report (IJR).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way to acquire citizenship in India ?
questions.explanation: Renunciation. There are five recognized ways to acquire citizenship in India under the Citizenship Act, 1955: By Birth - A person born in India can acquire citizenship by birth. By Descent - A person born outside India to Indian parents can acquire citizenship. By Registration - Certain persons, such as foreign nationals married to Indian citizens, can acquire citizenship through registration. By Naturalization - Foreign nationals can acquire citizenship after fulfilling certain residency requirements. By Incorporation of Territory - If a foreign territory becomes part of India.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following Sections of the Indian Penal Code deals with 'rape'?
questions.explanation: Section 375. Section 370 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) deals with the crime of human trafficking. Section 380 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) deals with theft in a dwelling house, tent, or vessel that is used as a human dwelling or for the custody of property. Section 385 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) deals with putting someone in fear of injury to commit extortion. According to BNS (Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita) Section for Rape is Section 63 and for Punishment for rape is Section 64.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Who is the Chief Executive Head of the State ?
questions.explanation: Governor. He is appointed by the President for a five-year term and holds office at the President's pleasure. The Governor has several key powers, including appointing the Chief Minister and other Ministers (Article 164), assenting or withholding assent to bills (Article 200), promulgating ordinances (Article 213), and granting pardons (Article 161).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: How many members (elected and nominated) were there in the Council of State under the Government of India Act 1919 passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom to expand participation of Indians in the government of India?
questions.explanation: 60. The Central Legislature was made more powerful and more representative by the Government of India Act, 1919. The Act made the Governor-General the chief executive authority. 26 nominated; 34 elected (20 General, 10 Muslims, 3 Europeans and 1 Sikh).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following was widely considered as the ‘heaven born service’ for Indians during British rule?

options.a: Military service on the Burma front
options.b: The Indian Civil Service or ICS

questions.answer_text: The Indian Civil Service or ICS
questions.explanation: The Indian Civil Service or ICS. It was brought into existence by Lord Cornwallis (1786-93) to check the corruption in the East India company (EEIC). The Charter Act of 1853 provided for Open competition for ICS examination. Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian to join ICS in 1863. Aitchson commission (1886) and Lee commission (1926) is related to reform in ICS.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following is the proposed successor to the Information Technology Act, 2000?
questions.explanation: Digital India Bill. The Digital India Act (DIA) aims to regulate the digital ecosystem, including cybersecurity, digital governance, and internet intermediaries. The Information Technology Act, 2000 (ITA-2000), notified on 17 October 2000, is India's primary law addressing cybercrime and e-commerce. Secondary legislation includes the Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2011, and the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The ‘Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana’ (‘PM-JAY’) scheme of the government is associated with which of the following Directive Principles of State Policy ?

options.a: Participation of workers in the management of industries
options.c: Equal justice and free legal aid
options.d: Duty of State to raise the level of nutrition and the improvement of public health

questions.answer_text: Duty of State to raise the level of nutrition and the improvement of public health
questions.explanation: Article 47 - Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the improvement of public health. Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy (Article 36 to 51): Article 38 - State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act: A. The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act was originally enacted in 1988. B. The Act was amended in 2016 and renamed as the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988. Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act was enacted in 1988 to prohibit benami transactions and recover property held benami. The 2016 amendment renamed it the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act and strengthened provisions for enforcement.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Who among the following founded an expatriate Communist Party of India at Tashkent in 1920?
questions.explanation: M.N. Roy (Father of Indian Communism). He was the first person to give the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India and the creator of the Mexican Communist Party. Communist Party of India (CPI) - It is the oldest communist party in India. Founded - in modern-day Kanpur on 26 December 1925. First General Secretary - S.V. Ghate . Headquarters - Ajoy Bhavan (New Delhi).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following Acts prevents disrespect to the National Flag and National Anthem?

options.a: Prevention of insults to National Honour Act, 1971

questions.answer_text: Prevention of insults to National Honour Act, 1971
questions.explanation: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971: Insults to Indian National Flag and Constitution of India - Whoever in any public place or in any other place within public view burns, mutilates, defaces, disfigures, destroys, tramples upon or into contempt the Indian National Flag or the Constitution of India or any part thereof, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In the Interim Government formed on 2 September 1946, Liaquat Ali Khan was given the charge of:
questions.explanation: The Finance Ministry. Interim Government (1946): Headed by Jawahar Lal Nehru. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel held the Home Affairs, Information, and Broadcasting. Rajendra Prasad held the portfolio of Agriculture and Food. C Rajagopalachari was the Education and Arts Minister. Jagjivan Ram held the Labour Ministry. Jogendra Nath Mandal was the Law Minister.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statement about the Government of India Act, 1935. 1. This act was enacted by the British Parliament. 2. This Act was divided into two separate acts for the India and Burma Government. 3. This act commenced from 1 April 1935. Select the correct statement(s) using the code given below.
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. The Government of India Act 1935 (Commenced in 1937): It provided for the establishment of an All India Federation consisting of provinces and princely states as units. It divided the powers between the Centre and units in terms of three lists, Federal List, Provincial List and Concurrent List.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Who propounded the concept of 'Rule of Law'?
questions.explanation: AV Dicey. Rule of Law - It means all laws apply equally to all citizens of the country and no one can be above the law. Three principles of Rule of Law given by A.V. Dicey : Supremacy of law, Equality before law, Individual rights. Chander Kishan Daphtary - First solicitor general of India (1950-63).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which of the following years was the Child Marriage Restraint Act passed?
questions.explanation: 1929. Child Marriage (The marriage of a girl or a boy before the age of 18 years). Prohibtion of Child Marriage Act (PCMA), 2006 :- It replaced the Child Marriage Restraints Act, 1929. The marriageable age to be 18 and 21 for girls and boys respectively Other laws to protect the child :- Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Justice Indu Malhotra penned a dissenting opinion in which of the following landmark judgements?
questions.explanation: Entry of women to Sabarimala. Justice Indu Malhotra opined that religious practices cannot be solely tested on the basis of Article 14. The right to equality under Article 14 does not override the fundamental right to religion under Article 25. The notions of rationality cannot be invoked in matters of religion. The Supreme Court struck down provisions of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965, and allowed women, irrespective of their age, to enter Sabarimala temple and worship the deity.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, amends the Income Tax Act of ________.
questions.explanation: 1961. Taxation Law Amendment Act, 2021 - It aims to withdraw tax demands made using a 2012 retrospective legislation to tax the indirect transfer of Indian assets. Income Tax Act (1961) - It provides an elaborate mechanism for the levying of taxes, their administration, collection & recovery. It has 298 sections & 14 schedules.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty Seventh Amendment) Bill, 2021, was introduced in the Lok Sabha by the ______ in August 2021.

options.a: Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment

questions.answer_text: Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment
questions.explanation: Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment - By Dr. Virendra Kumar. 102 Amendment Act, 2018: Constitutional status was provided to the National Commission for Backward Classes under Article 338B. Articles 338 and 338A - The National Commission for Scheduled Castes (SC) and National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (ST), respectively. 103rd Amendment Act, 2019:- Reservations for the Economic Weaker Section and amendment in Articles 15(6) and 16(6), provide 10% reservation in public employment.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Offences for which the police can arrest a person without an order from the court are called _________.
questions.explanation: Cognizable offenses - It includes murder, rape, theft, kidnapping, counterfeiting, etc. Detention - The act of temporarily holding individuals in custody or confinement, typically by a government or governing authority by removing their freedom or liberty at that time. Non-Cognizable offences - An offence for which a Police officer has no authority to arrest without warrant. These include offences like cheating, assault, defamation etc.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which act has been amended by the Supreme Court of India to provide equal rights to daughters in their ancestral property ?
questions.explanation: Hindu Succession Act (1956) - It governs the inheritance of property by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs. Contempt of Courts Act (1971) - It defines the power to punish for contempt of court and regulates their procedure. Hindu Marriage Act (1955) - It defines the minimum age of 18 years for the bride and 21 years for the groom.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which year was the Dowry Prohibition Act passed in India?
questions.explanation: 1961. Dowry Prohibition Act: It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Important Acts in India - Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856, Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929, Muslim Women Protection of Rights on Marriage Act 2019 (Triple Talaq Act), Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016, National Security Act 1980.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which year was the Arms Act passed in India?
questions.explanation: The Indian Arms Act of 1959: As per the preamble, this Act aims to consolidate and amend the law relating to arms and ammunition. The main objective of this Act is to regulate and restrict the circulation of arms and ammunition, which were illegal. It was enacted by the Indian government after independence, recognizing that certain law-abiding citizens must own and use firearms for sports, crop protection, and self-defence.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which year was the Special Marriage Act passed in India?
questions.explanation: 1954. Special Marriage Act (SMA) is an Indian law that provides a legal framework for the marriage of people belonging to different religions or castes. The applicability of the Act extends to the people of all faiths, including Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Jains, and Buddhists, across India. The minimum age to get married under the SMA is 21 years for males and 18 years for females.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In India, according to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the process of insolvency resolution for companies should be completed in how many days?
questions.explanation: 180. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) - A time - bound process for resolving insolvency in companies and among individuals. Objective - To consolidate and amend all existing insolvency laws, to simplify and expedite the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Proceedings, to promote entrepreneurship.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which year was the Indian Parliamentary Group established?
questions.explanation: In 1949, The Indian Parliamentary Group was an autonomous body formed in the year 1949 in pursuance of a motion adopted by the Constituent Assembly (Legislative) on 16th August 1948. Speaker of Lok Sabha is its ex-officio President.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: If the State government dissolves the Panchayati Raj Institutions before the end of their five-year term, fresh elections should ordinarily be held within _____.
questions.explanation: Six months. Under Article 243 E - An election to constitute a Panchayat shall be completed - Before the expiry of its duration specified in clause (1) or before the expiration of a period of six months from the date of its dissolution.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The detention of a person cannot exceed ________ unless an advisory board consisting of judges of a High Court reports sufficient cause for extended detention.
questions.explanation: three months. Article 22 (Part III) grants protection to persons who are arrested or detained (available to both citizens and foreigners). Preventive detention means the detention of a person without trial and conviction by a court.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: When was the National Emergency declared for the first time under Article 352 ?
questions.explanation: 1962-68. The National Emergency has been declared 3 times in India : 1962 to 1968 {During the India-China war, when “the security of India” was declared as being “threatened by external aggression”, President (Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan)}. 1971 {During the Indo - Pakistan war, President (V.V.Giri), Prime Minister (Indira Gandhi)}. 1975 to 1977 {The emergency was declared on the basis of “internal disturbance”, President (Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed), Prime Minister (Indira Gandhi)}.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which year was the National Youth Policy launched by the Government of India ?
questions.explanation: 2014. It seeks to define the Vision of the Government of India for the Youth of the Country. The first youth policy was released in 1988. National Youth Day is held every year on 12th January to observe the birth anniversary of Swami Vivekananda.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which freedom fighter abolished the Zamindari System in Uttar Pradesh and was elected as the Home Minister in 1955?
questions.explanation: Govind Ballabh Pant successfully abolished the exploitative Zamindari system and revolutionised laws pertaining to women’s inheritance and marriage. He was appointed Minister of Home Affairs in the Union Cabinet on 10 January 1955 in New Delhi by Nehru. He started a weekly paper called ‘Shakti’. In 1957, he was awarded the Bharat Ratna.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: As per the coding convention of India Census, how many digit code is used for showing state code?
questions.explanation: 2. The coding convention used: State code (2 digits); District code (3 digits); Sub-district code (5 digits); Village code (6 digits).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the National Emblem of India: A. The National Emblem of India was adopted on 26th January 1950. B. The emblem is adapted from the Sarnath Lion Capital of Ashoka and carries the motto “Satyameva Jayate” from the Mundaka Upanishad. Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both A and B. The National Emblem was officially adopted on 26th January 1950, is based on the Sarnath Lion Capital of Ashoka, and features the motto “Satyameva Jayate”, meaning “Truth Alone Triumphs,” from the Mundaka Upanishad.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 is an Act of Parliament which came into force in:
questions.explanation: 2010. The Act makes education a fundamental right of every child between the ages of 6 and 14 and specifies minimum norms in elementary schools.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In which of the following years was an Act enacted to provide for the reorganisation of the states of India and for matters connected therewith?
questions.explanation: 1956. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 was a major reform of the boundaries of India's states and territories, organising them along linguistic lines. The Government divided the country into 14 states and 6 union territories under the State Reorganisation Act.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following Acts was passed by the Government of India to inquire into allegations of corruption against certain public functionaries?
questions.explanation: The Lokpal and Lokayukta Act was passed by the Government of India to inquire into allegations of corruption against certain public functionaries.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Indian Forest Act 1927 was enacted after repealing which of the following Indian forest acts?
questions.explanation: Indian Forest Act, 1878. The Indian Forest Act of 1878 divided Indian forests into reserved forests (completely government-controlled), protected forests (partially government-controlled) and village forests (controlled by abutting villages).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the streams of charged particles ejected by the Sun into space called ?
questions.explanation: Solar wind. It is a constant stream of charged particles (mostly protons and electrons) that are released from the Sun's upper atmosphere, known as the corona. The solar wind blows in all directions. It continues moving at that speed for about 10 billion kilometers (six billion miles). Sunspots are dark surface spots, Solar flares are sudden bursts of energy, and Coronal loops are arcs of hot plasma shaped by magnetic fields.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following systems can be affected by a solar storm? 1. GPS signal accuracy 2. Power transmission systems 3. Submarine communication cables 4. Pipeline infrastructure
questions.explanation: 1, 2, 3, and 4 all of these. Solar storms release high-energy charged particles and electromagnetic radiation that disturb Earth’s magnetosphere. This can disrupt GPS accuracy, power grids, submarine cables, and pipelines by inducing currents and affecting signal transmission. Hence, all four listed systems are vulnerable.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. A solar eclipse- The Moon casts a shadow on Earth when it comes between the Sun and Earth. 2. A lunar eclipse- During the new moon phase, the Moon passes through the Earth's shadow. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation: 1 only. Statement 2 : Incorrect. A lunar eclipse occurs at the full moon phase, not new moon. It happens when the Earth comes between the Sun and Moon, and Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct sequence in the life cycle of a star like the Sun?

options.a: Protostar → White Dwarf → Red Giant → Main Sequence
options.b: Nebula → Red Giant → Main Sequence → White Dwarf
options.c: Main Sequence → Red Giant → White Dwarf

questions.answer_text: Main Sequence → Red Giant → White Dwarf
questions.explanation: Main Sequence → Red Giant → White Dwarf. The life cycle of a medium-sized star (like our Sun) follows a specific sequence: 1. Nebula / Protostar stage – Stars are born in large clouds of gas and dust (nebula). The contracting gas forms a protostar. 2.Main Sequence – The star spends most of its life in this stable phase, where hydrogen fusion occurs in the core (the Sun is currently in this stage). 3. Red Giant – After hydrogen in the core is exhausted, the star expands and cools to become a Red Giant. 4. White Dwarf – Finally, after shedding its outer layers (planetary nebula), the star’s remaining dense core becomes a White Dwarf.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Faint Young Sun paradox challenge our understanding of early Earth's climate?

options.a: It implies there was no liquid water on early Earth.
options.b: It proves the Moon once had an atmosphere.
options.c: It suggests that early solar output was too weak to prevent global freezing.
options.d: It shows Earth was too hot due to excessive solar radiation.

questions.answer_text: It suggests that early solar output was too weak to prevent global freezing.
questions.explanation: The Faint Young Sun paradox arises because about 4 billion years ago, the Sun’s luminosity was only around 70% of its current strength, which should have left Earth frozen. However, geological evidence shows that liquid water existed, supporting life’s early evolution. This paradox challenges climate science by suggesting that greenhouse gases or other warming mechanisms must have compensated for the weaker Sun, preventing global freezing and maintaining habitable conditions on early Earth.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of galaxy has no regular shape and is rich in gas and dust?
questions.explanation: Irregular Galaxy. Irregular galaxies are those that lack a distinct shape (unlike elliptical or spiral galaxies). They are often rich in gas and dust, making them sites of active star formation. Examples include the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) near the Milky Way. Elliptical Galaxy – Oval-shaped, contains older stars, and has little gas or dust. Lenticular Galaxies – A hybrid form between elliptical and spiral galaxies; disk-shaped but lacking significant spiral arms. Spiral Galaxy – Flat, rotating disk with spiral arms, contains gas, dust, and young stars (e.g., Milky Way).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which planet has the longest day in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Venus. A day on a planet is measured by its rotation period (time taken to complete one rotation on its axis). Venus rotates very slowly and in the opposite direction (retrograde rotation). One day on Venus (sidereal day) = 243 Earth days → the longest day in the solar system. Venus - Rotation period = 243 Earth days.Mars - Similar to Earth; 24 hours 37 minutes. Jupiter - Fastest rotation; ~9 hours 56 minutes (shortest day).Earth - 24 hours.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements about the Geoid: 1. The term Geoid refers to the axis of the Earth. 2. The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator due to the outward force caused by its rotation. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: 2 only. Geoid refers to the shape of the Earth, not its axis.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who gave the expanding universe hypothesis?
questions.explanation: Edwin Hubble. The most popular argument regarding the origin of the universe is the Big Bang Theory. It is also called the expanding universe hypothesis. Edwin Hubble, in 1920, provided evidence that the universe is expanding. As time passes, galaxies move further and further apart. Galileo Galilei is known for his contributions to astronomy, particularly with the use of the telescope.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the below statements is/are correct? Statement 1: Callisto, Europa, and Ganymede are natural satellites of Jupiter. Statement 2: Triton is the largest moon of Neptune.
questions.explanation: Both Statement 1 and 2. Jupiter, the most massive planet of the solar system and the fifth in distance from the Sun. Revolution - 11 years and 11 months, Rotation - 9 hours 56 minutes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is, by far, the closest dwarf planet orbiting at only 2.8 times Earth’s distance from the sun ?
questions.explanation: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and it is the only dwarf planet located in the inner solar system. It was the first member of the asteroid belt to be discovered when Giuseppe Piazzi spotted it in 1801.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements about a nebula: 1. A nebula is a cloud of dust and gas inside a galaxy, consisting mainly of hydrogen, helium, and other ionized gases. 2. Originally, the term nebula was used to describe only galaxies within the Milky Way. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: 1 only. The term nebula was originally used for any diffuse astronomical object, including galaxies outside the Milky Way.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A distinctive cross - shaped constellation best seen in the northern hemisphere during the summer and fall months around September is:
questions.explanation: Cygnus. It is a northern constellation on the plane of the Milky Way, deriving its name from the Latinized Greek word for swan.
