questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding planetary atmospheres: 1. Venus has thick white and yellowish clouds of sulphuric acid in its atmosphere. 2. Mars’ atmosphere is mainly composed of methane, with traces of sulfur dioxide. 3. Uranus is the coldest planet in the Solar System. 4. Venus is often referred to as the “morning star.” Which of the above statements is/are incorrect?
questions.explanation: Only 2. Mars, fourth planet in the solar system in order of distance from the Sun and seventh in size and mass. It is a periodically conspicuous reddish object in the night sky. Mars' atmosphere is 95.32% carbon dioxide, with methane and sulfur dioxide.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The colour of the surface of Mars is red because of the presence of large amounts of chemical compounds in it. What is the name of that compound ?
questions.explanation: Iron oxide. Mars appears reddish due to the presence of ferric iron in the form of red hematite (Fe2O3). The surface pressure of Mars is 610 Pascals, and its gravity is about one - third of Earth's. A Martian day lasts 24 hours and 37 minutes. Mars has two moons: Phobos and Deimos.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which dwarf planet orbits the sun in 310 years at a distance between 38.5 to 53 AU ?
questions.explanation: Makemake. It is the third-largest and second-brightest known dwarf planet. It was discovered in 2005. Pluto was discovered in 1930. It was initially classified as the ninth planet of the Solar System but was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. Pluto has a natural satellite named 'Charon'.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is the second nearest star to Earth?
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri. It is the closest star to the sun, at a distance of 4.24 light - years. A light - year is the distance light travels in one year, which is about 9.461 x 1012 kilometers. Polaris (North Star) is located nearly directly above Earth's North Pole along its rotational axis. Sirius (Dog Star) is the brightest star in Earth's night sky. Delta Velorum is a triple star system in the southern constellation of Vela.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements most accurately describes the planet Saturn?

options.a: It is a gas giant made up mostly of hydrogen and helium and the density is less than that of water
options.b: Its surface is reddish in colour.
options.c: It was the seventh planet discovered in the Solar System.
options.d: Its cloud-like outer regions consist of methane in the gaseous form and ammonia in crystalline form.

questions.answer_text: It is a gas giant made up mostly of hydrogen and helium and the density is less than that of water
questions.explanation: Saturn's density (0.70 gm/cm3 ) is less than that of water, making it the least dense planet in the solar system. If there were a body of water large enough, Saturn would theoretically float. The presence of methane and ammonia is more characteristic of Uranus and Neptune.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rocky planets is the fastest planet in our solar system – traveling through space at about 29 miles (47 kilometers) per second?
questions.explanation: Mercury. It is the nearest to the sun. It takes only about 88 days to complete one round along its orbit. Venus: It is considered as ‘Earth’s - twin’ because its size and shape are very much similar to that of the earth. Venus is also known as Lucifer. Earth is the fifth largest planet (in size). It is slightly flattened at the poles and its shape is described as a Geoid. Mars - The fourth planet from the Sun and it is a dusty, cold, desert world with a very thin

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the largest spiral galaxies?
questions.explanation: NGC 6872, which is one of the largest spiral galaxies, spanning 522,000 light-years across, approximately five times the size of the Milky Way. It is located 212 million light-years from Earth in the southern constellation Pavo.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Match the following planets with their approximate day length (rotation period): List I (Planet) List II (Day Length in Hours) A. Mercury i. 25 B. Venus ii. 1,408 C. Mars iii. 5,832 D. Neptune iv. 16
questions.explanation: A–ii, B–iii, C–i, D–iv. Planet and Day Length in hours: Mercury (1,408), Venus (5,832), Earth (24), Mars (25), Jupiter (10), Saturn (11), Uranus (17). Mercury is nearest to the sun. It takes only about 88 days to complete one round along its orbit.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who was the first to develop a mathematical predictive heliocentric model of the solar system ?
questions.explanation: Nicolaus Copernicus. Although Aryabhatta (5th century A.D.) hinted at astronomical ideas, Copernicus (1473 - 1543) developed the first mathematical heliocentric model, where planets revolved around a fixed Sun. Galileo supported this model, and Johannes Kepler later refined it by introducing elliptical orbits, now known as Kepler's laws.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who calculated the approximate location of the planet Neptune by studying gravity- induced disturbances in the motion of Uranus?
questions.explanation: Urbain - Jean - Joseph Le Verrier. He was a French astronomer and mathematician. Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet in our solar system, and it is the second coldest planet. It was discovered in 1846. It is the windiest planet in our solar system. One day on Neptune takes about 16 hours.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the below statements is/are correct? Statement 1: Apogee is the point in the orbit of an object around the Earth where it is farthest from the Earth’s center. Statement 2: Perigee refers to the point where the Moon’s orbit is closest to the Earth.
questions.explanation: Both Statement 1 and 2. Perihelion: The Earth closest to the Sun on 3rd January. Aphelion: The Earth farthest from the Sun on 4th July.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the below statements is/are incorrect? Statement 1: The Big Dipper is an asterism formed by the seven brightest stars in the constellation Orion. Statement 2: Ursa Major is the largest constellation in the entire sky.
questions.explanation: Both Statement 1 and 2. Statement 1 is incorrect because the Big Dipper belongs to the constellation Ursa Major, not Orion. Statement 2 is also incorrect because Ursa Major (Great Bear) is the third - largest constellation in the sky and the largest constellation in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A constellation of the northern sky easily recognised by a group of five bright stars forming a slightly irregular ‘W’ is called:
questions.explanation: Cassiopeia. It is a prominent constellation in the northern sky. It is visible during winter in the early part of the night. It looks like a distorted letter W or M.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Assertion (A): Saturn is the second largest planet in our Solar System and has the most prominent ring system. Reason (R): Saturn is larger than Jupiter and has Titan, the largest moon in the Solar System.

options.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.answer_text: A is true, but R is false.
questions.explanation: A is true, but R is false. Our Solar System has eight planets which orbit the sun. In order of distance from the sun they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Largest to smallest: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury. Saturn moon Titan is the second largest moon after Ganymede (Jupiter’s moon).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: _________ oblong orbit overlaps the orbit of Neptune.
questions.explanation: Pluto’s. Neptune is the outermost Jovian planet in the solar system. Until 2006 Pluto was the farthest planet from the Sun. In 2006, The International Astronomical Union (IAU) downgraded the status of Pluto to that of a dwarf planet. The Jovian planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, which are also known as the gas giants.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about planet Saturn is true?

options.a: Saturn is the fourth planet from the Sun and the largest planet in our solar system.
options.b: Satellites like Enceladus and Titan of Saturn are home to internal oceans, could possibly support life.
options.c: Saturn's environment is conducive to life.
options.d: Saturn is a massive ball made up mostly nitrogen.

questions.answer_text: Satellites like Enceladus and Titan of Saturn are home to internal oceans, could possibly support life.
questions.explanation: Saturn is the second largest planet, composed of hydrogen and helium. It has 146 moons. Titan - It is the largest moon of Saturn and the second largest moon in our solar system. Enceladus - It is the second nearest of the major regular moons of Saturn and the brightest of all its moons. It was discovered in 1789 by the English astronomer William Herschel. It is found that Titan has methane in its atmosphere and Enceladus has a liquid ocean with erupting plumes of gas and water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which star is also known as the ‘Pole Star’ ?
questions.explanation: The North star. Polaris, also known as the North Star, is located almost directly above Earth's north pole along our planet's rotational axis. The imaginary line that runs through the Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole is called the Earth's axis of rotation. The Earth rotates around this axis, similar to how a top spins around its spindle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In 1905, who concluded with Thomas Chamberlain that the planets of the Solar System originated from an encounter between the Sun and another star?
questions.explanation: Forest Moulton. He was an American astronomer and mathematician known for his contributions to celestial mechanics. He co-developed the Chamberlin-Moulton planetesimal hypothesis, which proposed a model for the formation of the solar system. According to this hypothesis, planets formed from smaller bodies called planetesimals through the process of accretion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Perihelion is when Earth is ______.
questions.explanation: nearest to the sun. On 3rd January, the earth is the nearest to the sun (147 million km). Aphelion is the point of the Earth’s orbit that is farthest away from the Sun.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the most widely accepted model to explain the formation and evaluation of the solar system?
questions.explanation: Nebular hypothesis - The planets were formed out of a cloud of material associated with a youthful sun, which was slowly rotating. The theory was developed by Immanuel Kant. But Mathematician Laplace revised it in 1796. Other Hypothesis: Big Bang Theory - Propounded by George Lamaitre related to the origin of the universe.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which trend is found about the distance between the galaxies?
questions.explanation: Increasing. In 1929, Edwin Hubble announced that almost all galaxies appeared to be moving away from us. He found that the universe was expanding - with all of the galaxies moving away from each other. This phenomenon was observed as a redshift of a galaxy's spectrum.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding terrestrial planets: 1. Terrestrial planets are primarily composed of rocks and metals. 2. Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are classified as terrestrial planets. 3. Terrestrial planets can be further categorised into silicate, iron, coreless, and carbon (diamond) planets. 4. The atmosphere of all terrestrial planets is primarily made up of hydrogen and helium. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only 1, 2 and 3. In our solar system, planets are broadly classified into two categories: terrestrial and Jovian. Terrestrial planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars) are small, rocky, and relatively close to the Sun. Jovian planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune) are gas giants, much larger and further from the Sun.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which scientist thought of the concept of the steady state of the universe?
questions.explanation: Fred Hoyle. Steady - State Theory : It is a theoretical model in which the Universe is constantly expanding but with a fixed average density. The theory was put forward by three scientists Sir Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold, and Sir Fred Hoyle in 1948.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the below statements is/are incorrect? Statement 1: Comets are cosmic snowballs of frozen gases, rock, and dust that orbit the Sun. Statement 2: Meteorites are stars that fall from space and burn completely before reaching the Earth’s surface.
questions.explanation: Only Statement 2. Meteorites - When a meteoroid survives its trip through the atmosphere and hits the ground, it’s called a meteorite. Meteorites typically range between the size of a pebble and a fist.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the radius of the earth?
questions.explanation: 6371 km. Earth Distance from the Sun (150 million km), Surface area: 510.1 million km², Land area: 149 million km², Gravity: 9.8 m/s².

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Each orbit of the International Space Station (ISS) takes _____minutes.
questions.explanation: 90-93. In 24 hours, the space station makes 16 orbits of Earth, traveling through 16 sunrises and sunsets.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Match the following planets with their approximate rotation period (one spin on its axis): List I (Planet) List II (Rotation Period) A. Earth i. 17 hours 14 min B. Jupiter ii. 1 day (23 hours 56 min) C. Saturn iii. 9 hours 56 min D. Uranus iv. 10 hours 40 min
questions.explanation: A–ii, B–iii, C–iv, D–i.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In early 1610, who discovered with his newly invented telescope that Jupiter has four moons?
questions.explanation: Galileo Galilei. He was an Italian astronomer and scientist. He described the rings of Saturn, the phases of Venus, sunsets, and the bumpy lunar surface. The four moons he discovered were: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who was the first to accurately describe the rings of Saturn as a disc around the planet in 1655?
questions.explanation: Christiaan Huygens. His other inventions include the pendulum clock, centrifugal governor, and magic lantern.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The moon completes _________ rotation on its axis as it completes one revolution around the Earth.
questions.explanation: 1. The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite circling the planet at an average distance of 384,400 kilometers. The Moon's presence helps stabilize our planet and moderate our climate. The radius of the Moon is 1.74 × 106 m. Huygens is the Moon's tallest mountain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the moon is correct? I. The size of the illuminated part of the moon visible from the Earth increases each day after the new moon day. II. After the full moon day, the sunlit part of the moon visible from the Earth decreases in size every day.
questions.explanation: Both I and II. When there are two full moons within a month, the second full moon is called a Blue Moon, When a full moon occurs at its perigee (the moon is closest to the earth) it is called a Supermoon.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The ______ radiation belts are giant swaths of magnetically trapped highly energetic charged particles that surround Earth.
questions.explanation: Van Allen. An aurora is a natural phenomenon which is characterized by a display of a natural-coloured (green, red, yellow or white) light in the sky.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which of the following periods is the meteor shower named Quadrantids generally visible from Earth?
questions.explanation: December / January. Quadrantids are best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere during the night and predawn hours. They are also known for their bright fireball meteors. The Quadrantids can produce over 100 meteors per hour in a moonless sky.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding solar eclipses: 1. A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun. 2. Types of solar eclipse include Total, Hybrid, Annular, and Partial. 3. In an annular solar eclipse, the Moon appears smaller than the Sun and does not completely cover it. 4. A penumbral eclipse is a type of solar eclipse. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only 1, 2 and 3. Penumbral (Lunar eclipse). A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun. Types of solar eclipse: Total (Completely blocking the face of the Sun), Hybrid (the Moon is farther away from Earth, it appears smaller than the Sun and does not completely cover the Sun) and Annular (when Sun is at or near its farthest point from Earth).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which of the following months may the meteor shower named Lyrids be seen from Earth?
questions.explanation: April. The radiant point for the Lyrid meteor shower is near the constellation Lyra, which has the bright star Vega in the east.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: At what latitude does the easterly jet stream blow over peninsular India during the summer months?
questions.explanation: 14°N. The Jet Stream is a geostrophic wind blowing horizontally through the upper layers of the troposphere, generally from west to east. The tropical easterly jet stream, located between 8 and 35 degrees north latitude, is connected to the southwest monsoon in India.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which month is the InterTropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) located around 20°N-25°N latitude (over the Gangetic plain) ?
questions.explanation: July. The Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a low pressure zone located at the equator where trade winds converge, and so, it is a zone where air tends to ascend. The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone located around 20°N-25°N latitudes (over the Gangetic plain) in July month is sometimes called the monsoon trough.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the below statements is/are incorrect? Statement 1:Longitude directly determines the temperature of ocean waters. Statement 2: Ocean currents influence ocean water temperature by transporting warm and cold water masses.
questions.explanation: Only Statement 1. Statement 1 is incorrect because longitude does not directly affect ocean water temperature. Factors determining ocean water temperature : Latitude - Affects the amount of solar radiation received. Unequal distribution of land and water - Affects heat absorption and distribution. Ocean currents - Transport heat and cold water masses globally.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding the Coriolis force?

options.a: It deflects the wind to the right in the north and left in the south.
options.b: It is directly proportional to the angle of altitude
options.c: Deflection is less when the wind is high
options.d: It is absent at the equator.

questions.answer_text: Deflection is less when the wind is high
questions.explanation: Deflection is less when the wind is high. Coriolis force : An apparent force caused by the earth’s rotation. The Coriolis force acts perpendicular to the pressure gradient force (pressure gradient force is perpendicular to an isobar). It is maximum at the poles and is absent at the equator. The Coriolis force also affects ocean currents.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the below statements is/are correct? Statement 1: The Torrid Zone lies between the Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) and the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S). Statement 2: The Frigid Zones are located between the Tropics and the Arctic/Antarctic Circles.
questions.explanation: Only Statement 1. The zones located between the Tropics and the Arctic/Antarctic Circles are the Temperate Zones. The Frigid Zones are the coldest regions, located between the Arctic Circle (66.5° N) and the North Pole, and between the Antarctic Circle (66.5° S) and the South Pole. The Torrid Zone experiences high temperatures year-round due to direct sunlight.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the Standard Meridian of India?
questions.explanation: 82°30ʹ E. The Standard Meridian of India, which passes through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, also crosses the following states: Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following sets of statements are correct about Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) ? A. The ITCZ is a broad trough of low pressure in equatorial latitudes. B. This is where the northeast and the southeast trade winds converge. C. The ITCZ is the equatorial trough normally positioned about 5°N of the equator and remains there throughout the year. D. The ITCZ moves over to the plane of Ganga in Summer.
questions.explanation: A, B and D. Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) - The region that circles the Earth, near the equator, where the trade winds of the Northern and Southern Hemispheres come together. Seasonal shifts in the location of the ITCZ drastically affects rainfall in many equatorial nations, resulting in the wet and dry seasons of the tropics rather than the cold and warm seasons of higher latitudes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: During October-November, the apparent movement of the sun is towards the _____.
questions.explanation: South. The position of the rising sun keeps on moving towards the south in the period from 21st June to 22nd December. This period is called Dakshinayan. From 22nd December to 21st June, the sun keeps on moving towards the north. This period is called Uttarayan.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Match the following waterbodies with the locations they separate: List I (Channel) List II (Separates) A. 8° Channel i. Andaman Islands and Nicobar Islands B. 9° Channel ii. Minicoy and Maldives C. 10° Channel iii. Minicoy & Lakshadweep main group D. 11° Channel iv. Amindivi Islands & Cannanore Islands
questions.explanation: A–ii, B–iii, C–i, D–iv.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The southern part of India lies in the _________ belt.
questions.explanation: Warm. The Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India. The southern parts being closer to the Equator, experience high temperatures throughout the year. The northern parts on the other hand lie in the warm temperate zone.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following states of India is NOT crossed by the Tropic of Cancer (23°30′ N)?
questions.explanation: Kerala. The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′ N) passes through eight states in India - Gujarat (Jasdan), Rajasthan (Kalinjarh), Madhya Pradesh (Shajapur), Chhattisgarh (Sonhat), Jharkhand (Lohardaga), West Bengal (Krishnanagar), Tripura (Udaipur) and Mizoram (Champhai).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: On which of the following two dates does the equinox fall ?
questions.explanation: 21 March and 23 September. Equinox is the situation when the equator receives the vertical rays of the Sun and day and night are equal. Spring equinox - 21st March, Autumn equinox - 23 September. 21st June (winter solstice in Southern Hemisphere, Summer solstice in Northern hemisphere) - The rays of the sun fall directly on the Tropic of Cancer. 22 December (Summer solstice in Southern hemisphere, winter solstice in Northern Hemisphere) - The rays of the sun fall directly on the Tropic of Capricorn.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: From the north most to south most point of India, what is the extent of India?
questions.explanation: 3214 km. Extent of India: East to west (2,933 km), land frontier (15,200 km), coastline (7,516.6 km). The westernmost point (Ghuar Moti in Kutch). The easternmost point (Kibithu in Arunachal Pradesh). Indira Col (northernmost point). Indira Point (Great Nicobar Island, Andaman sea) is the Southernmost point of India while Kanyakumari is the southernmost point of the Indian Mainland.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the zone between the arctic circle and north pole called?
questions.explanation: Frigid zone. The North Frigid Zone, between the North Pole at 90° N and the Arctic Circle at 66°33′48.7" N, covers 4.12% of Earth's surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. Isochrones are lines joining points located at equal travel time from a common centre. 2. Isohalines are lines connecting points of equal temperature in the ocean. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only 1. Isohaline - A line drawn on a map to indicate connecting points of equal salinity in the ocean. Isonomal - A line on a chart connecting points of equal abundance values of a plant species sampled in different sections of an area. Isobronts - A line drawn through geographical points at which a given phase of thunderstorm activity occurred simultaneously.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: 1° latitude is equal to approximately ______ km.
questions.explanation: 111 km. This distance decreases marginally as one travels to poles and increases marginally as one goes towards the equator.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the primary reason for the asymmetrical distribution of continents and oceans across the Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: The Earth's continents are fragments of a once-unified supercontinent (Pangaea) that have been continuously drifting, colliding, and rearranging due to the movement of tectonic plates. This dynamic process, driven by seafloor spreading at mid-ocean ridges and subduction at trenches, has resulted in the current, uneven arrangement of landmasses and ocean basins, such as the land-heavy Northern Hemisphere and the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The Arabian Sea, located in the North Indian Ocean, covers an area of about 3.86 million square kilometres. 2. The Arabian Sea has higher salinity due to high evaporation and low influx of fresh water. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. The North Indian Ocean is a region of the Indian Ocean that includes the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. The Red Sea is located between Africa and Asia. The Java Sea is located in Indonesia, between the islands of Java and Borneo. The Andaman Sea is located in the northeastern part of the Indian Ocean.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is the largest crustal plate on Earth with an area of over 103,000,000 km2 ?
questions.explanation: Pacific plate : It is the largest oceanic plate. Plate Tectonics theory given by McKenzie, Parker and Morgan in 1967. It proposes that the earth’s lithosphere is divided into seven major and some minor plates. Major plates : Antarctica and the surrounding oceanic plate; North American (with western Atlantic floor separated from the South American plate along the Caribbean islands) plate; South American (with western Atlantic floor separated from the North American plate along the Caribbean islands) plate; Pacific plate; India-Australia-New Zealand plate; Africa with the eastern Atlantic floor plate; Eurasia and the adjacent oceanic plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The Peninsular Plateau of India was earlier a part of the continent Africa. 2. The Peninsular Plateau of India was earlier a part of the continent North America. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.explanation: Only 2. The peninsular plateau of India was a part of the supercontinent Gondwana, which included Africa, South America, Australia, and Antarctica. After breaking up from Gondwana, the Indian subcontinent drifted northwards and collided with Eurasia which formed the Himalayas.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In the context of water bodies, Neap Tides occur :

options.a: when the earth, moon and sun line up in a straight line
options.b: when the sun and moon are on the opposite sides
options.c: when there is so much interference by continents
options.d: when the sun and moon are at right angles to each other

questions.answer_text: when the sun and moon are at right angles to each other
questions.explanation: During neap tide, gravitational and centrifugal forces are divided. The high tides of a neap tide are lower than the average high tide and the low tides of a Neap tide are higher than the average low tide. Spring tides - When the sun, the moon and the earth are in a straight line, the height of the tide will be higher. These are called spring tides, and they occur twice a month.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a landlocked Salt Lake in South-West Asia between Israel and Jordan?
questions.explanation: Dead Sea. Its salinity of 340 grams per litre of water. The Dead Sea seawater has a density of 1.240 kg/L, which makes swimming in its waters similar to floating. The Caspian Sea is the world's largest saltwater lake by volume. The Aral Sea is located between Kazakhstan to the north and Uzbekistan to the south.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which ocean is encircling the continent of Antarctica and extends northward to 60 degrees south latitude?
questions.explanation: Southern Ocean. It is the newest of the world's five oceans, officially designated as a separate ocean by the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) in 2000. The Atlantic Ocean is between the Americas and Europe/Africa. The Indian Ocean is between Africa, Asia, and Australia. The Pacific Ocean is between Asia and the Americas.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The name of the strait between the Pacific and Arctic oceans, separating the Chukchi Peninsula of the Russian Far East from the Seward Peninsula of Alaska, is the :
questions.explanation: Bering Strait. Davis Strait : It is located between Greenland and Baffin Island in Canada. It connects Baffin Bay with the Labrador Sea and is part of the Northwest Passage in the Arctic. Florida Strait : It is a channel of water located between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean, separating the Florida Keys and Cuba. Strait of Messina : It is a narrow passage between the eastern coast of Sicily and the western coast of Calabria in southern Italy. It connects the Tyrrhenian Sea with the Ionian Sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In 1596, who suggested in his work 'Thesaurus Geographicus' that the continents of the earth were not always located in their present positions ?
questions.explanation: Abraham Ortelius was a Dutch mapmaker who proposed in his work Thesaurus Geographicus that the continents were once joined together. This idea laid the groundwork for the continental drift theory, later fully developed by Alfred Wegener in 1912. Wegener suggested that all continents formed a single landmass called Pangaea ("all earth"), surrounded by a vast ocean known as Panthalassa ("all water").

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a part of the ocean floor?
questions.explanation: The deep sea shelf. A continental shelf is the submerged edge of a continent beneath the ocean. The continental slope extends seaward from the shelf to the upper edge of a continental rise or the point where the slope begins to flatten. An abyssal plain, or deep sea plain, is a flat region on the ocean floor, typically found at depths between 3,000 and 6,000 meters. Oceanic deeps are the deepest parts of the ocean, covered with fine-grained sediments such as clay and silt. Examples of oceanic landforms : Abyssal plains, Submarine canyons, Deep ocean trenches, Guyots, Seamounts, Mid-ocean ridges, Abyssal plains, etc.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The thermocline layer is the ______ layer of the ocean.
questions.explanation: Second. Scientists have divided the ocean into five main layers. Epipelagic Zone - The surface layer from the surface to 200 meters. Mesopelagic Zone - The twilight zone or the midwater zone. Bathypelagic Zone - The midnight zone or the dark zone. Abyssopelagic Zone - The water temperature is near freezing, and there is no light at all. Hadalpelagic Zone - The deepest point in the ocean is located in the Mariana Trench.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In 1962, who published 'The History of Ocean Basins', which outlined the theory of how tectonic plates could move, later called 'sea floor spreading' ?
questions.explanation: Harry Hammond Hess, an American geologist and naval officer. He discovered that the oceans were shallower in the middle and identified the presence of Mid Ocean Ridges, raised above the surrounding generally flat sea floor (abyssal plain) by as much as 1.5 km. Seafloor spreading is a geologic process in which tectonic plates—large slabs of Earth's lithosphere—split apart from each other.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct match between column-A and column-B ? Column - A (Elements in earth crust) Column - B (Total % in earth crust) i. Oxygen a. 8% ii. Silicon b. 28% iii. Aluminium c. 47% iv. Iron d. 5%
questions.explanation: i-c, ii-b, iii-a, iv-d. Abundances of other Element in the Earth’s Crust: Calcium (Ca) - 3.63%, Sodium (Na) - 2.83%, Potassium (K) - 2.59%, Magnesium (Mg) - 2.09% and others - 1.41%. Earth has three layers: crust (upper layer), mantle (middle layer), and core (lower layer).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Continental Shelf which is the shallowest part of the ocean has an average gradient of:
questions.explanation: 1° or even less. The Continental Shelf is the extended margin of each continent occupied by relatively shallow seas and gulfs. About Continental Shelf : The shelf typically ends at a very steep slope, called the shelf break. Their width varies globally, with an average of about 80 km, but can be narrower or even absent in some regions, such as the coasts of Chile and the west coast of Sumatra.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Living organisms have been on Earth for how much percent of Earth's history?
questions.explanation: 80%. Taking Earth's age as nearly 4.6 Billion Years (BY), instead of 13.7 BY from the Big Bang, unicellular life appeared nearly 3.8 BY ago. This percentage is 3.8/4.6 X 100 = 82.6%, nearly.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Choose the correct statement(s) related to ‘continentality’. A. The sea exerts a moderating influence on climate. B. As the distance from the sea increases, the people experience extreme weather conditions. C. As one goes from the surface of the earth to higher altitudes, the atmosphere becomes less dense and temperature decreases.
questions.explanation: A and B. Continentality (i.e. very hot during summers and very cold during winters) found in inland areas. Continental climates are common between 40° and 70° north latitude and experience large temperature differences between day and night.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements about oceanic trenches: 1. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean is the deepest point on Earth, with a depth of about 11,022 metres. 2. The Java Trench, located in the Indian Ocean, is deeper than the Tonga Trench in the Southwestern Pacific Ocean. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: 1 only. Java Trench (also known as the Sunda Trench): Located in the northeastern Indian Ocean, its maximum depth is approximately 7,725 metres. Tonga Trench: Located in the Pacific Ocean near the Tonga Islands, its deepest point (Horizon Deep) is approximately 10,882 metres. Other Trenches: Puerto Rico Trench (8,400 m) - Atlantic Ocean; South Sandwich Trench (7,432 m) - Southern Ocean.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does El Niño refer to ?
questions.explanation: Hot water current. The term El Nino (Little Boy in Spanish) - Warming of the ocean surface, or above-average sea surface temperatures, in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean on the coast of Peru. El nino leads to weakening of trade winds in a region. La Nina (Little Girl in Spanish) - The periodic cooling of ocean surface temperatures in the central and east-central equatorial Pacific.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following oceans is surrounded by the continent of North America and South America to the east?
questions.explanation: Pacific Ocean (world’s largest and deepest ocean): It represents 45 percent of the global ocean surface. The International Date Line (established in 1884) passes through the mid-Pacific Ocean. The Atlantic Ocean is surrounded by the continents of North and South America to the west, and Europe and Africa to the east. The Indian Ocean is bordered by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. Due to the attraction of the Sun and the Moon, ocean water generally experiences two high tides and two low tides in a day. 2. Diurnal tides occur when there are two high tides and two low tides each day. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only 1. When the Earth, Sun, and Moon line up, their gravitational power combines to make exceptionally high tides where the bulges occur, called spring tides, as well as very low tides where the water has been displaced. When the Sun is at a right angle to the Moon, moderate tides, called neap tides. There are generally three types of tides: Diurnal - One high and low tide each day, Semi-diurnal - Two high and low tides each day, and Mixed - Two high and low tides each day of different heights.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following oceans extends into the Mediterranean Sea ?
questions.explanation: Atlantic Ocean is the 2nd largest ocean in the world. The Mediterranean is an intercontinental sea spread between Europe, North Africa, and Western Asia and connected to the Atlantic Ocean through the strait of Gibraltar.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The mohororvicic (Moho) discontinuity separates ?

options.c: Earth's crust and the inner core

questions.explanation: Earth's crust and the mantle. Moho discontinuity - It occurs at an average depth of about 8 kilometers beneath the ocean basins and 32 kilometers beneath continental surfaces.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the correct sequence of oceans according to size (from largest to smallest) ?

options.a: Pacific Ocean > Antarctic Ocean > Indian Ocean > Atlantic Ocean
options.b: Pacific Ocean > Indian Ocean > Antarctic Ocean > Atlantic Ocean
options.c: Pacific Ocean > Atlantic Ocean > Indian Ocean > Antarctic Ocean
options.d: Pacific Ocean > Indian Ocean > Atlantic Ocean > Antarctic Ocean

questions.answer_text: Pacific Ocean > Atlantic Ocean > Indian Ocean > Antarctic Ocean
questions.explanation: Pacific Ocean, the world's largest, was named by Ferdinand Magellan. The International Date Line passes through it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The percentage of earth's water found in the oceans is _________.
questions.explanation: 97.2 percent. Water covers 71 percent of Earth's surface. Distribution of Earth’s water: Oceans (97.2%), Glaciers (2.1%), Groundwater (0.61 percent); Freshwater lakes (0.009 percent), Inland seas (0.008 percent), Soil Moisture (0.005 percent), Atmosphere (0.001 percent), Rivers (0.0001 percent). 2.7 % of earth’s water is fresh.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How thick is the lithosphere?
questions.explanation: 10 to 200 km. The lithosphere is the outermost and mechanical layer of the Earth that consists of the entire crust and the top-most portion of the mantle. Mechanically, the earth’s layers can be divided into lithosphere, asthenosphere (80-200 km), mesospheric mantle, outer core, and inner core.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The crust is the Earth's outermost layer that is less than ______ percent of Earth by mass, with oceanic crust and continental crust often consisting of more felsic rocks.
questions.explanation: 1. The average density of oceanic crust is 3.0 g/cm3 , while continental crust has an average of 2.7 g/cm3 . The mass of the continental crust is 2.195. The continental crust (about 30 km) is composed of lighter (felsic) sodium potassium aluminum silicate rocks, like granite. The oceanic crust (about 5 km) is composed of dense (mafic) iron magnesium silicate igneous rocks, like basalt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The movement of Earth's plates is classified into three main types of tectonic boundaries. 2. Convergent, divergent, and transform are the three primary types of plate movements. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. The movement of the plates creates three types of tectonic boundaries: convergent, where plates move into one another; divergent, where plates move apart; and transform, where plates move sideways in relation to each other.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Movement of fault lines can cause:
questions.explanation: An earthquake. It is a sudden shaking or trembling of the earth which lasts for a very short time. Earthquakes tend to occur at the boundaries of earth’s plates. These boundaries are known as fault zones. Over 80 percent of earthquakes occur around the edges of the Pacific Ocean, an area known as the 'Ring of Fire'. Instrument used for measuring Earthquake: Seismograph.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the average salinity of the Indian ocean?
questions.explanation: 35 o/oo (35 parts per thousand). Salinity is the amount of salt present in 1000 grams of water. A salinity of 24.7 % has been regarded as the upper limit to fix ‘brackish water’.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Tsunami is NOT caused by:
questions.explanation: Hurricanes. Tsunamis are giant waves caused by earthquakes or volcanic eruptions under the sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a warm current?
questions.explanation: Gulf stream current in the North Atlantic and the Kuroshio Current in the North Pacific are warm currents. Warm Currents - Alaskan Current, Tsushima Current, Brazilian Current etc. Cold Current - Labrador Current, Canary Current, Benguela Current, Falkland Current, South Indian Ocean Current, Okhotsk Current, Humboldt or Peruvian Current etc.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding oceanic landforms: 1. An Atoll is a group of islands found in tropical oceans, consisting of coral reefs and a central depression. 2. A guyot is a shallow body of water separated from the ocean by a barrier reef. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: 1 only. Guyot is an undersea mountain. Lagoons are shallow bodies of water that are separated from the ocean by a barrier reef. Seamounts are underwater mountains that rise above the ocean floor but do not reach the surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Ocean acidification is the ongoing decrease in the pH of the Earth’s oceans, caused by the uptake of ______ from the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide. Ocean acidification is the worldwide reduction in the pH of seawater as a consequence of the absorption of large amounts of carbon dioxide by the oceans. It results in the alteration of marine food chains and food supply to humans.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the lowest known point on Earth: 1. Challenger Deep is located in the western Pacific Ocean. 2. The Great Barrier Reef is the world’s largest coral reef located in Australia. 3. Factorian Deep is the deepest point in the Pacific Ocean. Which of the statements given above is incorrect?
questions.explanation: 3 only. The lowest known point on earth is called Challenger Deep, which is present in the Pacific Ocean. Factorian Deep is the new deepest point in Antarctica's Southern Ocean. The Great Blue Hole is a giant marine sinkhole off the coast of Belize.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In coastal areas, during the night, wind blows from land to sea because:

options.a: low pressure is created on land
options.d: high pressure is created at sea

questions.explanation: water cools slower than land. The wind blowing from land towards the sea is the Land breeze. The wind blowing from the sea towards the land is a sea breeze. Both are induced by differences that occur between the heating or cooling of the water surface and the adjacent land surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The process of seepage of water into the ground is called ____.
questions.explanation: Infiltration occurs when surface water enters the soil.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which water body covers an area of 1,55,58,000 𝑘𝑚 and makes up only 2 4.3% of the global ocean?
questions.explanation: Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world's five major oceans.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements about the Sargasso Sea: 1. The Sargasso Sea is the only sea in the world that does not have a land boundary. 2. It is located in the Pacific Ocean and is named after the presence of brown Sargassum seaweed. Which of the statements given above is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Only 2. The Sargasso Sea is the only sea in the world without a land boundary. It is bounded entirely by ocean currents (North Atlantic Gyre: Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Current, Canary Current, North Equatorial Current). Statement 2 is incorrect - Sargasso Sea lies in the Atlantic Ocean. It is named so because of the presence of brown Sargassum seaweed.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Match the following Seismic Zones of India with their characteristics: List I (Seismic Zone) List II (Characteristic) A. Zone II 1.Least seismically active region B. Zone III 2. Moderate seismic activity C. Zone IV 3. High seismic activity D. Zone V 4. Most seismically active region
questions.explanation: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4. The Bureau of Indian Standards has classified regions in India into 4 seismic zones on the basis of historical seismic activity. These are zones II, III, IV and V. The magnitude scale used to measure earthquakes ranges from 1 to 12.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The _____ is responsible for Earth's magnetic field.
questions.explanation: outer core. On Earth, flowing liquid metal in the outer core of the planet generates electric currents. The rotation of Earth on its axis causes these electric currents to form a magnetic field which extends around the planet.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding Gondwanaland: 1. Gondwanaland included present-day South America, Africa, Madagascar, India, Australia, and Antarctica. 2. North America was also a part of Gondwanaland. Which of the above statements is/are incorrect?
questions.explanation: 2 only. Gondwana was a large landmass, sometimes referred to as a supercontinent. The remnants of Gondwana make up around two-thirds of today's continental area, including South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, Zealandia, Arabia, and the Indian subcontinent. Neighbouring Countries of India

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is in geographical proximity to Sri Lanka?
questions.explanation: Only Karaikal. Karaikal is a town in the Union Territory of Puducherry. Sri Lanka, formerly known as Ceylon, is an island nation in South Asia. Located in the Indian Ocean, southwest of the Bay of Bengal, it is separated from the Indian peninsula by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait. Sri Lanka shares a maritime border with the Maldives to the southwest and India to the northwest.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following pairs do NOT share any borders?
questions.explanation: Bhutan and Meghalaya. The Indian states of West Bengal (183 km), Arunachal Pradesh (217 km), Sikkim (32 km), and Assam (267 km) share their boundaries with Bhutan. The Kingdom of Bhutan and the Republic of India are separated by a 699 km long, regional border.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following countries has the highest Hindu population after India?
questions.explanation: Nepal. After India, the next nine countries with the largest Hindu populations are, in decreasing order : Nepal, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the United States, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Assertion (A): New Moore Island, also known as South Talpatti, is geographically closest to Bangladesh. Reason (R): It is located in the Bay of Bengal near the maritime boundary between India and Bangladesh.

options.a: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.c: A is correct, but R is incorrect
options.d: A is incorrect, but R is correct

questions.answer_text: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The Maldives are located to the south of Lakshadweep Islands of India. 2. The capital of Maldives is Male. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. The Maldives are a group of coral atolls that were formed from the crowns of an ancient volcanic mountain range.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding boundary lines of India: 1. The McMahon Line is the boundary between India and China. 2. The Radcliffe Line forms the boundary between India and Pakistan. 3. The Durand Line separates Pakistan and Afghanistan. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: 1, 2 and 3. Pakistan shares a border with India, defined by the Radcliffe Line (International Border) and the Line of Control. India has 15,106.7 Km of land border and a coastline of 7,516.6 Km including island territories. India shares the longest border with Bangladesh about 4,096.7 km and Shortest with Afghanistan about 106 km. The Durand line separates Pakistan and Afghanistan.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which trek in Bhutan is considered to be the crown jewel of Bhutanese trekking?
questions.explanation: Snowman Trek. It is a 27 day track. Other Treks in Bhutan - Jumolhari Trek, Dagala Thousand Lakes trek, Laya Gasa Trek, Druk Path Trek, Tsaluna Trek, etc. Treks in India - Kalindi Khal Trek, Stok Kangri Trek, Auden's Col Trek, Chadar Trek, etc.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Sino–Indian border (LAC): 1. The Line of Actual Control (LAC) is divided into three sectors – Western, Central, and Eastern. 2. The Eastern sector of the LAC lies across Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand states. Which of the above statements is incorrect?
questions.explanation: 2 only. The Indian Military has divided the LAC (Line of Actual Control) into 3 sectors - Western sector across Ladakh and the Chinese-held Aksai Chin, The central sector across Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand states, and the eastern sector across Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh states.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Match the following mountain passes with the countries/borders they are associated with: Pass Country / Border A. Khyber Pass 1. India–China border B. Pangsau Pass 2. India–Myanmar border C. Karakoram Pass 3. Pakistan and Afghanistan border D. Zojila Pass 4. India (Ladakh –Srinagar link)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The Sunderban forest is part of the world's largest delta and contains the largest mangrove forests. 2. The Sunderban forest is shared between India and Bangladesh. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. Sunderban forest is the only mangrove habitat in the world for Panthera tigris species.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rivers forms a delta along the Eastern Coastal Plains ?
questions.explanation: Godavari. The Godavari River, also called the Dakshina Ganga or Ganga of the South, forms a large delta along the Eastern Coastal Plains before draining into the Bay of Bengal. It is the second longest river in India after the Ganga. Major delta-forming rivers on the east coast: Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri. On the other hand, west-flowing rivers like Narmada, Tapi, and Mahi do not form deltas; they form estuaries because of their short course and fast flow into the Arabian Sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of these rivers does not originate in the Peninsular Plateau of India ?
questions.explanation: Ganga. The Ganga River does not originate in the Peninsular Plateau. Instead, it originates from the Gangotri Glacier in the Himalayas at Gaumukh in Uttarakhand. Origins of the other rivers : Godavari — Trimbakeshwar near Nasik, Maharashtra (Western Ghats). Krishna — Mahabaleshwar near Jor village, Maharashtra (Western Ghats). Cauvery (Kaveri) — Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri Hills, Karnataka (Western Ghats).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Ghaghara River system: 1. The Ghaghara originates from the Mapchachungo glacier in the Himalayas. 2. It forms a deep gorge at Shishapani before entering the plains. 3. It merges with the Ganga at Allahabad after receiving the Sarda River. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only 1 and 2. The Ghaghara River originates from the Mapchachungo glacier in the Tibetan Himalayas. It carves a deep gorge at Shishapani before entering the plains of Nepal. Statement 3 is incorrect because the Ghaghara joins the Ganga river near Chhapra in Bihar, not at Allahabad.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The Alaknanda River originates from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Satopanth Glacier. The Alaknanda River, a major tributary of the Ganga, originates from the Satopanth Glacier near Badrinath in Uttarakhand, at an elevation of about 3,650 metres. It flows through important confluences (prayags) such as Vishnuprayag, Nandprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag, and Devprayag, where it finally meets the Bhagirathi River to form the Ganga. In contrast, the Gangotri Glacier is the source of the Bhagirathi River, the Zemu Glacier feeds the Teesta in Sikkim, and the Milam Glacier gives rise to the Goriganga in Uttarakhand.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Read the given below statements carefully and choose the correct option: Assertion (A): The Chambal River is known for its badland topography called the Chambal ravines. Reason (R): The Chambal flows through a deep gorge and eroded terrain before joining the Yamuna.

options.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.answer_text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.explanation: The Chambal basin is famous for deep ravines formed due to intensive gully erosion, a classic example of badland topography. The Chambal indeed flows through a rugged, eroded landscape, cutting gorges and ravines before meeting the Yamuna in Etawah district (U.P.).The badland topography (ravines) is formed because of severe erosion by the river and its tributaries in the soft alluvial soils of the Chambal basin. Hence, the reason correctly explains the assertion. Chambal and its tributaries (Kalisindh, Banas, Sindh) intensify erosion. These ravines stretch across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an erosional landform created primarily by river action?
questions.explanation: Gorge. A gorge is a deep, narrow valley with steep sides, formed when a river cuts vertically into its bed through the process of erosion, especially in the upper course where the river has a steep gradient. It is a classic erosional landform created by river action. Moraine – Depositional landform created by glaciers, consisting of rock debris. Delta – Depositional feature formed at the river’s mouth due to deposition of sediments. Levee – A natural or artificial embankment formed alongside a river, also depositional in nature.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the evolution of India's major drainage systems: 1. The ancient Indo-Brahma river is believed to have split into three major drainage systems over time. 2. The Ganga and its Himalayan tributaries represent the central drainage system. 3. The western drainage system consists of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only 1 and 2. The Indo-Brahma River system is believed to be an ancient unified river that later broke into three drainage systems: the Indus (western), the Ganga (central), and the Brahmaputra (eastern). The Ganga and its Himalayan tributaries like Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, and Kosi form the central drainage system. However, the Brahmaputra and its tributaries constitute the eastern drainage system, not the western one.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which river is the main source of water for the Hirakud Dam?
questions.explanation: Mahanadi River. The Hirakud Dam, located near Sambalpur in Odisha, is built across the Mahanadi River. It is one of the world’s longest earthen dams (25.8 km) and serves multiple purposes—irrigation, hydroelectric power generation, and flood control in the Mahanadi delta.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The Jog Falls in Karnataka is formed from which river?
questions.explanation: Sharavathi. Jog Falls, also called Gerosoppa Falls or Joga Falls, is one of the highest plunge waterfalls in India (about 253 meters). It is located in Shivamogga district, Karnataka. It is a major hydroelectric power source as well, with the Sharavathi Hydroelectric Project built nearby. Godavari – Flows mainly through Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh. Kaveri – Famous for Shivanasamudra and Hogenakkal Falls, not Jog Falls.Krishna – Flows through Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh; associated with Almatti and Srisailam dams.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Trishulganga is a stream of the river:
questions.explanation: Gandak. It comprises two streams, namely Kaligandak and Trishulganga. It rises in the Nepal Himalayas between the Dhaulagiri and Mount Everest and drains the central part of Nepal. It enters the Ganga plain in Champaran district of Bihar and joins the Ganga at Sonpur near Patna.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Select the odd one from the following saltwater lakes on the basis of their formation?
questions.explanation: Sambhar lake: The largest inland saltwater lake in India situated in Rajasthan. Pulicat lake (Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu), Kolleru lake (Andhra Pradesh), and Chilika lake (Odisha) - are all coastal saltwater lakes, formed by the seawater entering the lake through creeks or rivers.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The Zaskar and the Nubra are tributaries of which river?
questions.explanation: Indus (Sindhu) originates from a glacier near Bokhar Chu in the Tibetan region at an altitude of 4,164 m in the Kailash Mountain range. Tributaries - Chenab River, Jhelum River, Ravi River, Satluj River, Beas River, Shyok River, Gilgit River, Hunza River, Swat River, Kunnar River, Kurram River, Gomal River, and Kabul River.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rivers flows north of the Tropic of Cancer in India?
questions.explanation: Yamuna. Originates - Yamunotri Glacier, Flows through the Himalayan foothills before entering the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Tributaries - Tons, Hindon, Chambal, Sind, Betwa, and Ken. The Yamuna River joins the Ganges River near Prayagraj (Allahabad). The Mahi River is the only river in India that crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice. Originates in the Vindhya Mountains in Madhya Pradesh, flows through Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Gujarat, and drains into the Arabian Sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the origin of major Indian rivers: 1. The spout emerging from the mouth of a cow statue in the Mahadev Temple at Mahabaleshwar is considered the source of the Krishna River. 2. The Godavari River originates from Trimbakeshwar in the Nashik district of Maharashtra. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. Krishna is the second largest east flowing Peninsular river which rises near Mahabaleshwar in Sahyadri. Origin of rivers : Kaveri - originates at Talakaveri, which is located on the Brahmagiri range in the Kodagu (Coorg) district of Karnataka. Narmada - rises from Maikala range near Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the salt measurement in hypersaline lagoons?
questions.explanation: More than 100. Hypersaline lagoons are extreme environments with salt concentrations significantly higher than typical seawater. While normal ocean salinity is around 35 parts per thousand (3.5%), hypersaline lagoons can have salt concentrations exceeding 100 parts per thousand (10%). These environments are typically found in arid regions with high evaporation rates and limited water input, such as the Dead Sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which state of India is kund or Tanka used for water harvesting ?
questions.explanation: Rajasthan. This region faces extreme arid conditions and low rainfall, so local communities have developed innovative systems to conserve and store water. Water harvesting structures in other States: Kere (large tanks) in Karnataka, Cheruvu in Andhra Pradesh, Bandharas and Tals in Maharashtra, Surangam in Kerala, Eris (tanks) in Tamil Nadu, Bhundis in Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding continental shelves: 1. The Siberian shelf in the Arctic Ocean is the largest continental shelf in the world. 2. A continental shelf is the edge of a continent that lies under the ocean. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. A continental shelf is the edge of a continent that lies under the ocean. Continents are the seven main divisions of land on Earth. A continental shelf extends from the coastline of a continent to a drop-off point called the shelf break. Example of a Continental Shelf Landform: Siberian Shelf, Arctic Ocean.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is the transboundary river between India and Pakistan?
questions.explanation: Ravi. This river flows through north-western India and eastern Pakistan. It, along with the Beas and Sutlej rivers, was allocated to India under the Indus Water Treaty. Indus River : This river originates in western Tibet, passes through Kashmir, and flows into Pakistan before falling into the Arabian Sea. It, along with the Chenab and Jhelum rivers, was allocated to Pakistan under the Indus Water Treaty of 1960.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which state of India was the Neeru-Meeru programme introduced for construction of water harvesting structures?
questions.explanation: Andhra Pradesh. The Neeru-Meeru (Water and You) program was launched by the Water Conservation Mission (WCM), on May 1, 2000. It was a Water conservation and poverty alleviation initiative.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Identify a water-harvesting system found in Jaisalmer.
questions.explanation: Khadins. ‘Rooftop rainwater harvesting’ was commonly practised to store drinking water, particularly in Rajasthan. In arid and semi-arid regions, agricultural fields were converted into rain fed storage structures that allowed the water to stand and moisten the soil like the ‘khadins’ in Jaisalmer and ‘Johads’ in other parts of Rajasthan. In hill and mountainous regions, people built diversion channels like the ‘guls’ or ‘kuls’ of the Western Himalayas for

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rivers marks the eastern-most boundary of the Himalayas ?
questions.explanation: Brahmaputra River flows through the northeastern part of India, originating from the Angsi Glacier in Tibet and passing through Arunachal Pradesh before entering Assam. The Teesta River rises in the Pauhunri Mountain of the eastern Himalayas and flows through the Indian states of Sikkim and West Bengal. The Satluj River originates in Raksas Tal near Mansarovar in Tibet. The Kali River flows through the Uttara Kannada district of Karnataka.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following peninsular rivers falls into the Arabian Sea?
questions.explanation: Sabarmati river. It is one of the major west-flowing rivers in India. It originates from Aravalli hills. Mahanadi river: Origin - Sihawa (South of Amarkantak) near Raipur (Chhattisgarh). It flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha and drains into the Bay of Bengal.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The Yamuna, Gandak, and Kosi are important tributaries of the river Ganga. 2. The Lohit River is not a tributary of the Ganga; rather, it is a tributary of the Brahmaputra. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both 1 and 2. The river Ganga emerges from Gangotri Glacier and ends at Bay of Bengal. Ganges is the longest river of India. It is 2,525 km long. Its tributaries include Yamuna, Gandak, Ramganga, Son, Ghaghra, Gomti, Kosi, Tamsa, Punpun, and Mahananda. Brahmaputra river originates under the name of Siang or Dihang, from the Chemayungdung glacier of the Kailash range near the Mansarovar lake. It enters India west of Sadiya town in Arunachal Pradesh. Tributaries: Dibang, Lohit, Siang, Burhi Dihing, Tista, and Dhansari.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following are west flowing rivers?
questions.explanation: Mahi and Sabarmati. Mahi River originates from Vindhyachal Hills, Madhya Pradesh and meets in Bay of Khambhat. Major West-flowing rivers - Indus, Narmada, and Tapi. Major East-flowing rivers: Ganga, Brahmaaputra, Mahanadi, Krishna, and Godavari. Major peninsular rivers - Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Narmada, and Tapti.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rivers is an east flowing river?
questions.explanation: Godavari river. It rises in the Nasik district of Maharashtra and discharges its water into the Bay of Bengal. It is 1,465 km long with a catchment area spreading over 3.13 lakh square kilometers. The Penganga, the Indravati, the Pranhita, and the Manjra are its principal tributaries. The Mahi (Origin, Northern slope of Vindhyas), Narmada (Origin, Amarkantak), and Tapi (Origin, Betul) rivers flow westward, draining into the Arabian Sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The confluence of the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers is at Devaprayag. 2. The Mandakini river meets the Alaknanda at Karnaprayag. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: 1 only. The Five Prayags are sacred river confluences in Uttarakhand. At Devaprayag, the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers meet. At Rudraprayag, the Mandakini and Alaknanda rivers converge. At Nandaprayag, the Nandakini joins the Alaknanda. At Karnaprayag, the Pindar meets the Alaknanda, and at Vishnuprayag, the Dhauliganga merges with the Alaknanda.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which state of India has the maximum number of large dams?
questions.explanation: Maharashtra leads in large dams, followed by Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat. Major dams in Maharashtra include Jayakwadi, Koyna, and Radhanagari. India's first dam, Kallanai, was built over 2,000 years ago. Notable post-independence dams include Hirakud (1957), Gandhisagar (1960), Bhakra-Nangal (1963), and Nagarjuna Sagar (1967).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which group of states does the Luni River flow?
questions.explanation: Rajasthan and Gujarat. The Luni River begins near Pushkar valley in two branches called the Saraswati and the Sabarmati. These two branches merge at Govindgarh, and from there, the river flows out of the Aravalli as the Luni. It continues westward until Telwara, then turns southwest to join the Rann of Kutch (Gujarat).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the land of Sapta Sindhu mentioned in Vedic literature: 1. The Aryans lived in the land known as Sapta Sindhu, meaning the land of seven rivers. 2. The seven rivers included Indus, Sutlej (Sutudri), Ravi (Parusni), Chenab (Asikni), Jhelum (Vitasta), Beas (Vipas), and Saraswati. 3. The Shipra River, flowing through Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh, was also one of the rivers of Sapta Sindhu. Which of the above statements is/are incorrect?
questions.explanation: 3 only. The Shipra (Kshipra), a 195 km tributary of the Chambal River in Madhya Pradesh, flows across the Malwa Plateau, passing through Ujjain, Ratlam, and Mandsaur before joining the Chambal. The Sapta Sindhu, mentioned in Vedic literature, refers to the "Land of Seven Rivers" in Punjab, home to early Aryan settlements.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rivers originates from the Himalayas?
questions.explanation: Ganga. Origin: Gangotri glacier near Gaumukh (3,900 m) in the Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand. Here, it is known as the Bhagirathi. It cuts through the Central and the Lesser Himalayas in narrow gorges. At Devprayag, the Bhagirathi meets the Alaknanda; hereafter, it is known as the Ganga (length 2,525 km). Other river origin: Godavari - Brahmagiri hills; Tapi - Satpura range; Narmada - Maikal ranges.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Subansiri, Jia Bharali, Dhansiri and Puthimari are the major tributaries of which river?
questions.explanation: Brahmaputra. The principal tributaries of the rivers are as follows: Godavari: Pravara, Purna, Manjra, Penganga, Wardha, Wainganga, Pranhita (the combined flow of Wainganga, Penganga, and Wardha), Indravati, Maner, and Sabri. Mahanadi: Seonath, Hasdeo, Mand, and Ib join Mahanadi from the left, while Ong, Tel, and Jonk join from the right. Bhagirathi: Bhilangna River, Kedar Ganga, Jadh Ganga, etc.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: On which river in India was the Somasila Dam built?
questions.explanation: Pennar river. It originates in the Nandi Hills, Karnataka, and flows through Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh before emptying into the Bay of Bengal. The Somasila dam is situated in the Nellore district (Andhra Pradesh). Famous dams and the rivers they are built on: Koyna Dam (Koyna River), Idukki Dam (Periyar River).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: The largest inland salt lake ‘Sambhar’ is located in the ______of India.
questions.explanation: north - west. Sambhar Salt Lake (located in Rajasthan) spans 230 square kilometers. It is a significant depression in the Aravalli Range and is commonly referred to as the salt lake of Rajasthan. The lake receives water from six rivers: Mantha, Rupangarh, Khari, Khandela, Medtha and Samod.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rivers is called ‘Singi Khamban’ in Tibet?
questions.explanation: Indus. It enters Pakistan near Chilas in the Dardistan region. Brahmaputra: Originates from the Chemayungdung glacier in the Kailash range and is known as Tsangpo in Tibet. Sutlej: Originates near Mansarovar in Tibet, where it is called Langchen Khambab. River Kosi: Originates near Mount Everest and is known as the sorrow of Bihar due to frequent flooding.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Match the pair correctly: National Waterways Stretch a) NW-1 1. Kakinada - Puducherry b) NW-2 2. Kottapuram- Kallam c) NW-3 3. Allahabad - Haldia d) NW-5 4. Sadiya- Dhubri 5. Talcher - Dhamra
questions.explanation: a-3, b-4, c-2, d-5. NW-1 is the longest waterway in India, stretching 1,620 kilometers from Haldia to Allahabad. NW-69 is the smallest (5 km) waterway in India. It is part of the Manimuthar River in Tamil Nadu.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding Chilika Lake: 1. Chilika Lake is located to the south of the Narmada delta. 2. It is Asia’s largest brackish water lagoon and India’s first Ramsar wetland site (1981). Which of the above statements is/are incorrect?
questions.explanation: 1 only. Chilika Lake is located to the south of the Mahanadi delta. Chilika Lake, Asia’s largest and the world’s second-largest lagoon, spans Puri, Khurda, and Ganjam districts in Odisha. Nalabana Island, a bird sanctuary, lies in the middle of Chilika Lake, while Satapada, where the lake meets the Bay of Bengal, is home to Irrawaddy dolphins.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Delhi ridge is the water divide between which of the following rivers?
questions.explanation: Ganges and Indus. The uplift of the Potwar Plateau during the Pleistocene upheaval in the western Himalayas rises the Delhi ridge. The major water dividers of India: Vindya range: Divided the Ganga drainage basin and Narmada river valley. Satpuda range: Divided Narmada river and tapi river valley.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the canal systems and Doabs of Punjab: 1. The Bist Doab Canal System lies between the Sutlej and Beas rivers. 2. The Makhu Canal System, built in 1950, draws water from the Sutlej river. 3. Doab Bari lies between the Beas and Chenab rivers. Which of the statements given above is incorrect?
questions.explanation: 3 only. Punjab's Doab systems include: Doab Chaj (Chenab and Jhelum), Doab Rachna (Ravi and Chenab), Doab Bari (Beas and Ravi, also called Majha), and Suj Doab (Satluj and Yamuna, part of the Malwa region).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of Indian rivers is west flowing?
questions.explanation: Narmada and Tapi. Narmada River (Rewa River), the longest west-flowing river, originates from the Maikal ranges and flows through Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Maharashtra. The Tapi River, the second-largest west flowing river, originates from Betul district in Madhya Pradesh and flows parallel to the Narmada. Other important west-flowing rivers include Periyar, Bharathappuzha, Netravati, Sharavathi, and Mandovi.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Match the following dams with the rivers on which they are built. a. Hirakud Dam (i) Chambal river b. Nagarjuna Sagar Dam (ii) Narmada River c. Sardar Sarovar Dam (iii) Krishna River d. Tehri Dam (iv) Mahanadi river e. Rana Pratap Sagar dam (v) Bhagirathi river
questions.explanation: a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-v, e-i. The Hirakud Dam, one of the longest in the world, is located near Sambalpur District, Odisha. The Nagarjuna Sagar Dam, a masonry dam, spans the border between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The Sardar Sarovar Dam, a concrete gravity dam, is situated near Kevadiya in Gujarat's Narmada District. The Tehri Dam, a multi-purpose rock and earth-fill embankment dam, is in New Tehri, Uttarakhand. The Rana Pratap Sagar Dam, a gravity masonry dam, stands 53.8 meters high in Rawatbhata, Rajasthan.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following rivers is joined by river Chambal from the south?
questions.explanation: Yamuna. It rises from the Yamunotri Glacier in the Himalayas. It flows parallel to the Ganga and as a right the bank tributary meets the Ganga at Allahabad. Its biggest tributary is Chambal River on the right. Other important tributaries include the Hindon, Sarda, and Giri rivers on the right and Betwa and Sindh on the left.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Choose the coasts that are running along the Arabian sea. A. Northern Circars, B Malabar, C. Konkan, D. Coromandel
questions.explanation: Only B and C. The western coast, between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, is a narrow plain with three sections: Konkan (Mumbai to Goa) in the north, Kannad Plain in the center, and Malabar Coast in the south. On the Bay of Bengal side, the plains are wide and level, called the Northern Circar in the north and the Coromandel Coast in the south.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which river flows into the Wular lake in the north and then into Baramulla?
questions.explanation: Jhelum River originates from a spring at Verinag in the southeastern part of the Kashmir Valley. It first flows northward into Wular Lake, located in the northwestern part of the valley. After leaving Wular Lake, it changes direction, flowing southwards. At Baramulla, the river enters a gorge in the hills, carving a steep-sided narrow passage through the Pir Panjal Range below Baramulla. Eventually, it merges with the Chenab River at Trimmu.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which river originates from ‘Rakshastal north-western tip’ near Mansarovar ?
questions.explanation: Sutlej River enters India through the Shipki La Pass in the Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh. It is an east bank tributary of the Indus River, meeting the Indus at Mithankot in Pakistan. Also known as Shatadru in ancient times, the Satluj is the only Indus tributary originating from Tibet. The Bhakra-Nangal Dam is built across the Satluj, and the Indira Gandhi Canal also draws water from it.

questions.subject: Geography
